CHAPTER-II 
 
OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF DEMANDS FOR GRANTS 
 
2.1 Overview 
 
2.1.1 There are eleven Demands for Grants which are administered by the Ministry of Home  
Affairs  (MHA). The detailed Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Home Affairs are divided into 
two volumes: Vol. - I and Vol. - II. The Detailed Demands for Grants (Volume-I) contains three 
Grants (Nos. 48-50), namely the Ministry of Home Affairs (Grant No. 48); the Cabinet (Grant No. 
49);  and the  Police  (Grant No. 50). The Detailed Demands for Grants (Volume-II) contains ei ght 
Grants (Nos. 51-58) that pertain to the eight Union Territories. 
 
2.1.2 The Demands for Grants (Vol. II) (Nos. 51-58) relate to the five Union Territories without a 
Legislature, namely Andaman & Nicobar Islands (Grant No. 51), Chandigarh (Grant No.52), Dadra 
and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu (Grant No. 53) (the UT of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and UT 
of Daman and Diu have been merged into a single UT since 26 th January, 2020), Ladakh (Grant. No 
54) and Lakshadweep (Grant No. 55). The remaining three Grants are Transfers pertaining to the 
three Union Territories with Legislature viz. Transfer to Delhi (Grant No. 56), Transfer to Jammu & 
Kashmir (Grant No. 57) and Transfer to Puducherry (Grant No. 58). 
 
2.1.3 The provisions for the Union Territories (without Legislature) form part of the Demands of 
the Ministry of Home Affairs. However, various programmes/schemes are the subject matter of 
different Ministries, which are responsible for scrutinizing, sanctioning and implementing the 
schemes/projects falling under their respective purview. Provisions for the Union Territories (with a 
Legislature) cover Assistance to the Union Territories of Puducherry, Jammu & Kashmir and NCT 
of Delhi, in the form of the Grants and Loans. In respect of these three Grants , the Ministry of 
Home Affairs releases the Grants on a quarterly basis and has a limited role in scrutinizing, 
sanctioning and implementation of the schemes/projects. 
 
2.1.4 While discussing the DFG (2021-22) for MHA in the meeting of the Committee held on 16 th 
February, 2021, the Home Secretary informed the Committee that one of the highlights during the 
period for the Budget in 2020-21 was the creation of two separate Grants for two new UTs i.e. 
Grant No. 54 for UT of Ladakh and Grant No. 57 for UT of J&K. This year, the allocations have 
been maintained at the same level for these UTs i.e. Rs.5,958 crore for Ladakh and Rs.30,757 crore 
for J&K.  The Committee was informed that the MHA has not only taken effective measures to 
contain the spread of the COVID-19 Pandemic, but also achieved some of the important activities 
despite the Pandemic and lockdowns. The National Police University has been established. The 
Rashtriya Raksha University (RRU) Bill has been passed in Parliament and the University has also 
commenced its operations from 1 st October, 2020. This University will meet the country's 
requirements for a pool of trained professionals with specialized knowledge and new skill sets in 
various wings of policing, criminal justice and correctional administration.  The National Forensic 
Sciences University has also commenced its operations from 1 st October, 2020. This University will 
meet the need for high-quality manpower in the field of forensic sciences.  Considerable progress 
has been made during the year in the Crime and Criminal Tracking Network System (CCTNS). Its 
software has now been deployed in 15,774 Police stations and 100% of FIRs are digitally recorded 
in more than 15,600 police stations. The States/UTs have launched their State Citizen Centre portals 
and so far 6.15 crore service requests have been handled on this portal. Besides this, the MHA is 
implementing the scheme of the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) which was 
launched last year to effectively deal with cyber crime in a coordinated and sustained manner.    

6 
 
2.1.5 The Home Secretary further informed the Committee that ensuring safety for women and 
children remains the topmost priority for the Government. The Safe City Project has been 
implemented which includes smart policing and safety management. The Emergency Response 
Support System (ERSS) 112 has ensured a citizen-friendly Emergency Response Mechanism.  By 
March 2021, all States and UTs except the State of Bihar will be covered by 112 ERSS System. 
Bihar would be covered in another five to six years' time.  The MHA has also focused on the 
Border Infrastructure and during the FY 2020-21, the Indo-China Border Road Phase - II 
programme has been sanctioned.  This programme covers many roads, foot tracks and Border out 
Posts (BoPs). Besides, for the borders especially with Bangladesh & Pakistan, considerable 
progress has been made in fencing, floodlighting, development of roads and BOPs. Two new 
Integrated Check Posts have also been added during the year.  In the North East, important 
settlements were reached during Financial Year 2020-21. A decision was taken to settle Bru 
(Reang) migrants in Tripura.  These people of the Bru (Reang) tribe fled to Tripura from Mizoram.  
They were to be resettled in Mizoram but could not go back and were being sheltered in Tripura. 
The process of their settlement has been started and a package of approximately Rs.661 crores has 
been allocated for the same.  These people would get all the rights that normal residents of the 
States get and they would now be able to enjoy the benefits of social welfare schemes of  Central 
and State Governments (Source: PIB). A  Memorandum of Settlement was also signed with the 
National Democratic Front of Bodo Land (NDFB) in January, 2020  and the long overdue Bodo 
Land issue was resolved.  Many cadres surrendered their weapons and elections to the Bodo Land 
Territorial Councils were held subsequently.  
2.1.6 In the Union Territory of J&K, three-tier Panchayati Raj System has been established.  The 
District Development Council (DDC) elections were conducted successfully in the 20 Districts of 
J&K and DDCs are in the process of formation now.  Further, there has been a decline in LWE 
violence over a period of time and its geographical spread. This is reflected in the reduction of 
incidents by about 70% over the last decade. Besides the COVID-19 Pandemic, the Ministry has to 
deal with many national calamities including severe cyclones like Cyclone Amphan, Nisarg & 
Nivar which struck coastal States of India. The situation was promptly monitored and necessary 
support was provided to the State Governments.  Moreover, to deal with the recent tragedy in 
Uttarakhand, the MHA is coordinating with the State Government along with various Central 
Government agencies.   
2.1.7 On Immigration Visa and Foreigners' Registration & Tracking (IVFRT) system, the M HA 
has made a lot of progress.  The e-visa facility, before COVID-19 Pandemic, was ex tended to 
foreigners of 171 countries. For foreigners already in India, the visa-related services has been made 
completely online. The process of issuance of OCI cards has also been made completely onli ne. In 
the current year and the coming year, the MHA will strengthen the installation of electronic gates, 
initially in Delhi and Mumbai, for pre-vetted and trusted travelers who can just scan their passports 
and boarding pass and walk through the gates without any human interface.   
2.1.8 The Department of Official Language is working hard to promote the Hindi language.  It 
has developed a framework of 12 P namely Prerna, Protsahan, Prem, Puraskar, Prashikshan, 
Prayog, Prachar, Prasar, Prabandhan, Promotion, Pratibaddhta and Prayas.  The Scheme of 
Assistance to State for Modernization of Police Forces is a critical scheme for the operational 
efficiency of the State Police Forces. Through this Scheme, the State Police forces have be en able 
to take a long-term view of the challenges faced and the strategies needed to address them. These 
strategies encompass state-of-the-art equipments, upgradation of forensic capacity or capacity 
building. The Government of India has also provided sufficient funds for the modernization of 
Central Armed Police Forces through a separate Scheme called Modernization Plan for CAPFs.

2.1.9 Regarding underutilization of funds during FY 2020-202q, the Home Secretary informed 
the Committee that because of COVID-19 Pandemic, there were some curtailments and restrictions 
on the use of funds every month as the Government was keeping a watch on outgo.  Due to this, 
there has been under-utilization under few heads. 
2.1.10 The Committee sought to know about the status of COVID-19 vaccination in the country. 
The MHA replied that COVID-19 vaccination drive is ongoing across all States and UTs from 16th 
January, 2021 for Health Care Workers and from 2nd February 2021 for Front Line Workers.   As 
on 18th February, 2021, a total of 98.46 lakh vaccine doses have been administered which include 
62.34 lakh 1st dose to Health Care Workers, 4.65 lakh 2nd dose to Health Care Workers and 31.47 
lakh 1st dose to Front Line Workers. Further, the ongoing vaccination drive is fastest in the world 
to achieve 1-7 million vaccinations across the world and in terms of total number of vaccinations 
administered till date, India is at 4th position across the world despite starting around a month later 
than other countries (Source: http://www.ourworldindata.org). 
 
2.1.11 Further, regular reviews are being undertaken with States and UTs for increasing the pace of 
vaccination drive and advisories have been issued to them on various operational aspects of 
COVID-19 vaccination. A Communication strategy has been developed for implementation at the 
National and State level to raise awareness about the safety, efficacy and immunogenicity of 
COVID-19 vaccines through prompt and consistent dissemination of factual information and to 
address misinformation related to it. The strategy is based on five key pillars- viz, advocacy , 
capacity building, media engagement, community engagement and crisis management.  The 
strategy aims to leverage peoples‟ ownership (Jan Bhagidaari) in taking the awareness about 
vaccination drive and its intended benefits forward. 
 
2.1.12 For successful implementation of the strategy, several measures have been taken so far. 
These include capacity building of stakeholders at National and State level including State 
Immunisation  and IEC officials, Civil Society Originations, Radio including Community Radio 
professionals, etc. for leveraging their networks for active campaigning to create awareness a bout 
benefits of vaccination.  Aggressive advocacy to build vaccine confidence have been done through 
reputed public and private sector Doctors at National level and in States/Union Territories (UT) 
who have received vaccination and through other key influences.  Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare is also carrying out real time review of news reports and developing and disseminating 
content on building confidence in vaccines and counter less  than adequate informed media 
narrative.  A special campaign against vaccine hesitancy has also been launched. The Ministry also 
reached out to 22 Central line Ministries including Rural Development, Panchayati Raj, Ministry of  
Information and Broadcasting and MyGov etc. for engaging their field level networks to support 
information dissemination and social mobilization. 
 
2.1.13 The Committee also enquired about the status of vaccination in Lakshadweep. The MHA 
replied that the UT has started vaccination in all islands on 16the January, 2021. The vaccination of 
health care workers and front line workers is almost completed. The UT has received a total of 
5,910 doses of COVID vaccine in four installments. 
 
2.1.14 The Committee notes that despite COVID-19 Pandemic and lockdowns, the Ministry 
has undertaken some important activities during the year 2020-21. The Committee 
appreciates the achievement of MHA that inter-alia includes establishment of Rashtriya 
Raksha University (RRU) implementation of Emergency Response Support System (ERSS) 
and CCTNS, conducting District Development Council (DDC) elections in Union Territory of 
J&K, Immigration Visa and Foreigners' Registration & Tracking (IVFRT) system, 

8 
 
resettlement of Bru (Reang), upgradation of forensic capacity or capacity building , 
modernization of Police forces, etc. 
2.1.15 The Committee takes note of the ongoing vaccination process for COVID-19. and 
observes that, till now, less than 1% of the Indian population has been vaccinated and at this 
rate it will take many years to vaccinate whole population. The Committee also expresses its 
concern that a large number of people are missing the second dose of the vaccine. The  
Committee believes that it is very serious issue as the virus is mutating and new variants of 
COVID-19 are being reported in different parts of the world. The Committee there fore, 
recommends that all frontline health workers and the Corona Warriors including CAPFs and 
State/UT Police personnel receive the recommended doses of vaccine.  An at tempt should be 
made to cover maximum people as early as possible. 
 
2.1.16 The Committee also recommends that vaccination in Lakshadweep can be don e for 
everyone as the population is very small (70 thousand approx.). As the medical facilities are 
limited, priority needs to be given for vaccination in Lakshadweep.

2.2.3 The MHA informed the Committee that the major thrust areas for the financial year 2021-
22 are conducting the Census, updation of NPR, modernization and strengthening of NDRF and 
other CAPFs, ensuring the safety of women and children, containing Left-wing extremism, 
modernization of State police forces and strengthening of border infrastructure. Depending on the 
progress and review of the work, additional funds would be sought at the RE stage. 
 
2.2.4 The Committee notes that there has been allocation of Rs. 1,03,802.52 crore for the 
Police (Demand No.50) at BE 2021-22. The allocation made for the Police (Demand No.50) 
under the Revenue Head is Rs.  94,086.59 crore and under Capital Head is Rs.  9,715.93 
crore at BE  2021-22. The Committee observes reduction in allocation for the Police 
Infrastructure, MoPF, BADP, SRE, Infrastructure for LWE and LPAI in BE 2021-2 2 over 
BE 2020-21. This may hamper the creation of assets and negatively imp act the capabilities 
of the Police forces . The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Minis try should 
reconsider the requirements of the funds for the Po lice and Union Territories and pursue 
with the Ministry of Finance for increased allocati on at the Revised Estimates stage. The 
Committee further recommends that the MHA should also constantly mon itor the 
utilization of funds under different heads on a quarterly basis and ensure op timal utilization 
of funds. 
2.2.5 The Committee notes that the total allocation for the Union Territories in BE 2021-22  
is Rs. 55,006.73 that is divided into two parts. i.e. Union Territories (without legislature) is Rs. 
21,562.43 crore and Union Territories (with legislature) are Rs. 33,444.30 crore. Further, for 
the Union Territories (without legislature), the allocation under the Revenue Head is Rs. 
15,657.52 crore i.e. 72.61% of the total allocation to the UTs and Capital Head is Rs. 5,904.91 
crore i.e. 27.38% of the total allocation to the UTs. The Committee is of the considered view 
that the allocation under the Capital Head for the Union Territories (without legislature) 
should be increased for infrastructure in Health, Education, Agricultural, Energy and Allied  
sectors, Transport (connectivity), Development of Tourism, etc., in the UTs. The Committe e, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry must review the capital requirements of these UTs 
and demand appropriate enhancement at RE stage to carry out developmental work s in the 
UTs.

3.8 Glacial Outbursts 
 
3.8.1 The Committee showed its concern towards glacial outbursts in the Himalayan region and 
sought to know about the monitoring system for such glacial outbursts. The MHA replied that the 
Government of India has a good system of monitoring avalanche movement etc. There are various 
agencies under the Ministry of Science and Technology. Even Defense Research and Deve lopment 
Organization (DRDO) has an agency called Snow & Avalanche Study Establishment (SASE) 
which works in avalanche forecasting, artificial triggering, and structural controls in snow-bound 
mountainous areas. All the agencies coordinate to make predictions and forecasts. The forecast and 
the avalanche warning bulletins issued by SASE are disseminated through Army Network 
(AWAN) for the Indian Army and DRDO/ NDMA website for the civilian population. After 
receiving the forecast bulletin from SASE, National Emergency Response Center (NERC) also 
shares the same with Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs) and State Governments concerned. 
 
3.8.2 The avalanche forecast is being generated on daily basis by Snow and Avalanche Study 
Establishment (SASE) which is based on models/ algorithms, developed by DRDO. The inputs for 
these models are snow and meteorological data collected on a daily basis by the army jawans from 
field observatories and the automatic weather stations spread across the Himalayas. These 
Forecast bulletins are sent to Defence Forces and concerned State Governments/ SDMAs.  
 
3.8.3 NDMA had also released Guidelines on Management of Glacial lake Outbursts Flows 
(GLOFs), Summary for Policy Makers and Compendium of Task Force Report, in collaboration 
with Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC), Swiss Embassy India and experts of 
Task Force; on 13 th October 2020. The purpose of the development of GLOF guidelines is to 
encourage the use of scientific information, maps, methodology & guidance for the early warning 
system, response management, development and implementation of initiatives to reduce losses 

19 
 
from glacial hazards involving concerned States/ UTs and other stakeholders. These Guidelines 
also describe the awareness, preparedness, capacity development, research & developme nt, 
regulations & enforcements and roles & responsibilities of the local, State/UT and national 
Ministries/Departments along with the various scientific organizations and institutions to reduce 
the potential risks. An online webinar on „New Strategies to Mitigate the Risk of GLOFs Related 
Disasters in Indian Himalayan Region‟ was conducted on 11 th December, 2020 on the occasion of 
International Mountain Day, in which more than 100 participants participated. 
 
3.8.4 The Ministry vide its reply to a query raised in the meeting of the Committee held on 16 th 
February, 2021 has informed `that monitoring of GLOF would require a network of meteorological 
and hydrological stations, which will provide real-time data on air temperature, precipitation and 
river discharge through telemetry (V-SAT). Further bathymetry of potentially hazardous lakes 
would also be beneficial to estimate the impact in vulnerable regions. Avalanches can be monitored 
using snowpack characteristics on the ground. However, remote sensing data can provide 
information on changes in the area of the glacial lakes and help in preparing baseline data of 
potentially hazardous glacial lakes and avalanches. 
 
3.8.5 The early warning system should comprise of remote Automatic Water Level Recorder 
(AWLR) or Monitoring Stations and Automatic Weather Stations (AWS) with the ability to 
communicate and transmit data from remote stations to the control room for operation and 
monitoring in real-time. It should also have several sirens to warn vulnerable communities along 
the river valley downstream. The control station operators should be able to view the latest data 
from any of the stations using custom-developed software for decision making. 
 
3.8.6 Further, the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology (WIHG) is currently monitoring eight 
(8) glaciers so far namely Gangotri, Dokriani, Chorabari, Dunagiri, Bangni, Pindari, Kafni, 
Sunderdunga in Uttarakhand and two (2) glaciers in Doda and Suru valley of J&K. The WIHG has 
also initiated glaciological studies in the Karakoram region. The studies include glacial retreat, 
mass balance, meteorology, hydrology and hydrochemistry. However, the present observations are 
restricted to the summer season (May – October) due to harsh weather conditions in winters and 
logistical limitations. WIHG has also prepared glacial lake inventory for Uttarakhand and Himachal 
Pradesh using remote sensing and geographical information system (GIS). 
 
3.8.7 The Committee was further informed by MHA that the first step to disseminate early 
warning to the local people is by sensitizing and generating awareness in the local communities 
about such disasters and the standard operating procedures to be followed. Further, the information 
from early warning systems should be directly monitored by the administrative and disaster 
response agencies like district administration, state disaster relief force for rapid response. Also, the 
early warning system should be equipped with sirens along the river valleys to alert the vulnerable 
communities in downstream.  
 
3.8.8 The Committee notes that Monitoring of Glacial Lake Outbursts Flows (GLOFs) 
requires a network of meteorological and hydrological stations, early warning system 
comprising of remote Automatic Water Level Recorder (AWLR) or Monitoring Stations an d 
Automatic Weather Stations (AWS) with the ability to communicate and transmit data from  
remote stations to the control room etc., for operation and monitoring in real-time data on air 
temperature, precipitation and river discharge through telemetry (V-SAT). 
 
3.8.9 The Committee observes that the Himalayan region of Ladakh, Jammu & Kashmir, 
Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand are young, fragile and sensitive mountains. Therefor e, 
there is a need to establish and install state-of-the-art infrastructure along with modern  

20 
 
equipments of proven efficacy and reach that would play very crucial role in mon itoring the 
movement of glaciers in Himalayan region. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Ministry of Home Affairs should emphatically put before the Ministry of Finance its spe cific 
requirements for the purpose and seek appropriate budgetary allocation at  the RE stage. 
 
3.8.10 In view of the recent severe glacial outburst at Chamoli in Uttarakhand, the 
Committee, strongly recommends that for ensuring safety of the people of Himachal Pr adesh, 
Uttarakhand and Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, a network of meteorological and 
hydrological stations, monitoring stations and weather stations be set up at the earliest. The 
Committee, also recommends that an urgent assessment needs to be made and organizations 
like Indian Institute of Remote Sensing, Dehradun, Uttarakhand, may also be tasked to 
conduct glaciological studies and prepare glacial lake inventory for Himalayan region using 
remote sensing and geographical information system (GIS). Besides, the concerned Stat es 
should be sensitized by the MHA to place adequate early warning mechanism in every district 
so that vulnerable communities can be alerted on the wake of any disaster in future. 
 
3.8.11 The Committee observes that excessive cutting of trees and use of dynamites on  
Hills/Mountains of the Himalayan region for roads, tunnels, dams and other 
developmental/infrastructural projects is significantly weakening the surrounding hills and 
may be causing an avalanche, landslides, flash floods and other catastrophes. The Comm ittee 
understands that the Himalayas are fragile mountains and geologically and environmentally 
sensitive. Therefore, the developmental projects taking place in the region should b e 
considered from the environmental and ecological point of view. The Committee recommen ds 
that the MHA may coordinate with the concerned agencies including NDMA, Ministry of 
Road, Transport & Highways, etc. to immediately ban the use of dynamites for 
developmental projects in the Himalayan region and make judicious use of technology 
particularly in high altitude Himalayan region to minimize the damage to ecology and 
environment. The Committee further recommends to explore technological solutions 
including use of cutting-edge technology and best practices followed by the othe r countries 
for cutting of hills/mountains for various developmental projects.

3.11 National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project (NCRMP) 
 
3.11.1 The National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project (NCRMP) was launched to address the 
cyclone risks in the country with World Bank assistance. The objective of NCRMP is to strengthen 
the structural and non-structural cyclone mitigation efforts. NCRMP has been approved in two 
phases: Phase-I and Phase-II. The four components of the project are- Early Warning Dissemination 
System (Component A), Cyclone Risk Mitigation Infrastructure (Component B), Technical 
Assistance for cyclone hazard risk mitigation, capacity building and knowledge creation 
(Component C), and Project Management and Implementation Support (Component D). 
Components A, B, C, D are fully funded by the Centre and Component B is shared in the ratio of 
75: 25 between the Centre and the States.

 3.11.4 The various studies towards technical Assistance on Capacity Building undertaken in 
NCRMP phase- II include a study on National Seismic Risk Mitigation Program (NSRMP). The 
objective of NSRMP is to reduce the vulnerability of communities and their assets to a natural 
disaster by taking appropriate mitigating measures and to strengthen the capacity of National and 
State entities to effectively plan for and respond to earthquakes.  NSRMP is intended to cover nine 
(09) high-risk States/UTs viz., Assam, Bihar, Himachal Pradesh, J&K, Ladakh, Manipur, 
Meghalaya, Tripura and Uttarakhand.  A Detailed Project Report (DPR), Bid document and other 
supporting documents are to be prepared under the programme (NSRMP). 
 
3.11.5 The Technical study intends to design NSRMP as a futuristic step and aims at reducing the 
vulnerability of communities and their assets to a natural disaster by taking appropriate mitigation 
measures and strengthening the capacity of national and state entities to effectively plan for and  
respond to earthquakes in 09 States/UTs. 
 
3.11.6 This Contract for Preparation of National Seismic Risk Mitigation Programme (NSRMP) is 
awarded to M/s DDF-AKDN JV (a joint venture between DDF Consultants Private Limited (DDF) 
and Aga Khan Agency for Habitat India (AKDN). The Contractor (i.e. JV) has already submit ted 
(Deliverable 1) i.e. Inception Report.  Further, the Initial project scoping report (Deliverable 2) and 
Draft Environmental and Social Management Framework (ESMF) document (Deliverable 4) which 
was also submitted by the contractor, was initially examined by NDMA and has been returned to  
the contractor for revision in both the deliverables.  A model DPR on technical and environmental 
aspects is also submitted by the contractor.     
 
3.11.7 The Committee was further informed by MHA that a Comprehensive National Earthquake 
Risk Mitigation Project (CNERMP) has been formulated. It covers a wide spectrum of activities, 
ranging from techno-legal regime to retrofitting of critical infrastructure and lifeline buildings and 
structures, in the high earthquake risk zones (namely Seismic Zones IV and V). The on-going 
National Seismic Risk Mitigation Programme (NSRMP) under National Cyclone Risk Mitigation 
Project (NCRMP Phase-II) acts as a preparatory phase for CNERMP. NSRMP‟s scope of work 
broadly consists of preparing detailed Project Reports, formulating implementation arrangements 
and preparing necessary documents such as environment and social assessment reports, operation 
manuals, bidding documents, etc. The work has been awarded for Phase-I, for carrying out the

above-mentioned preparatory work. The total financial outlay for the NSRMP is Rs. 45 crore. The 
project will be implemented in highly earthquake-prone areas of the country in two phases. Phase-I 
will include 7 states- Assam, Bihar, Himachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Tripura, Uttarakhand 
and phase –II will include four states/UTs.-Delhi, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim. Another three 
states/ UTs of Arunachal Pradesh, J&K and Ladakh will be taken up out of National Disaster 
Mitigation Fund. The proposed financial outlay is Rs. 4082.96 crore with a duration of 5 years. 
50% of the fund will be provided by the World bank.

Early Warning Dissemination System (EWDS) work has been awarded in Goa, Karnataka 
and Kerala. The Committee also observes the decrease in allocation in RE 2020-21 due to 
very slow progress of project works because of strict restrictions put in place to contain the 
spread of COVID-19 Pandemic. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the work may 
be expedited for Phase-II of NCRMP in the ensuing year so that the installation and 
Commissioning of EWDS are completed in projected time without cost overruns and S tates 
are equipped to deal with the Cyclones at the earliest.

3.14 Disposal of Enemy Property 
3.14.1 The Committee sought to know about the steps taken for disposal of enemy property. The 
MHA replied that an amount of Rs. 3,172 crore (approx.) has already been realized through the sale 
of moveable properties such as Gold & Silver jewellery, Shares, Bonds and Securities. The sale of 
remaining shares of some unlisted companies is also being processed. The number of Immoveable 
Enemy properties vested in the CEPI on date is 12,610. A majority of these properties are 
encroached upon and under litigation. The mechanism of disposal has now been streamlined and a 
graded system of disposal involving the District valuation committees and District Collectors has 
been set up. Only properties that are free of litigation and encroachments and are above Rs.100 
crore in value will be referred to DIPAM. The smaller properties with a value of less than ₹1 crore 
would be disposed off by District Collectors, either to the occupiers or to the highest bidder, if the 
occupier is not willing to purchase it or pay for it. All the remaining properties would be disposed 
off by CEPI through online auction. With this new system in place and subject to the resolution of 
litigation, substantial progress is expected in the next couple of years.  The following steps are 
being taken to speed up progress of disposal of Enemy Properties- 
 
a. It has been decided to dispose all properties upto Rs.1 crore by offering the same to 
occupier/occupiers to dispose the same through e- auction after evicting the 
occupiers.  
b. All encumbrance free properties would be disposed by e- auction.  
c. MoU is being negotiated with MSTC for e- auctioning the properties.  
d. VC has been held with 18 States' Nodal Officers and concerned DMs for carrying 
out time bound Survey, Valuation and Eviction act about Enemy Properties in their 
respective jurisdictions.  
e. Efforts are being made to expedite disposal of court cases involving Enemy 
Properties.  
f. No fresh lease agreements are being made in respect of all properties which have 
been leased out to private people.  
g. Action is being taken to take over all leased properties in which lease agreement 
period has terminated.

the measures taken by the Government to dispose off enemy properties and recommen ds to 
take necessary steps to remove encroachment and expedite the disposal of remaining en emy

4.3.23 Regarding the reasons for stress among CAPF personnel, the MHA replied that 
studies/investigations have been carried out in the past for assessment of the factors responsible for 
causing stress in Forces and suggest remedial measures for the same. One such study wa s 
conducted by BPR&D in 2004. Further, the Indian Institute of Management, Ahmadabad (IIMA) 
did a similar study in 2012 for BSF & CRPF. Some of the measures taken to reduce stress and 
improve working conditions among CAPFs and AR personnel are as follows:- 
 

39 
 
(i) Transparent policies pertaining to transfer and leave of CAPFs and AR personnel. The 
hospitalization period due to injuries while on duty is treated as on duty.  Choice posting is 
considered to the extent possible after the personnel served in hard area. 
(ii) Regular interaction of officers with troops to find out and redress their grievances. 
(iii) Ensuring adequate rest and relief by regulating the duty hours. 
(iv) Improving living conditions for troops, providing adequate recreational/ entertainment, 
sports, communication facilities etc. Crèche facility is also provided at various 
establishments (where feasible) to facilitate the female employees. 
(v) Facility of retention of government accommodation at the place of last posting (for keeping 
the family) while posted in NE State, J&K and LWE affected areas (except State Capitals). 
(vi) Providing better medical facilities, also organizing talks with specialists to address their 
personal and psychological concerns and organizing Meditation & Yoga routinely for better 
stress management. 
(vii) Adequately compensating the troops deployed in difficult areas. 
(viii) Other welfare measures like facility of Kendriya Police Kalyan Bhandar (KPKB),  
scholarship for wards etc.  
(ix) Air travel to Non Entitled category posted/deployed in J&K. Air courier services have also 
been provided to CAPF personnel deployed in NE States, J&K and LWE affected areas as 
welfare measure. 
(x) Designating retired CAPF personnel as ex-CAPF personnel for better identity and 
community recognition. 
(xi) Promotions are released regularly to eligible personnel as & when the vacancies arise. 
Financial benefits under Modified Assured Career Progression (MACP) are given in case 
promotion does not take place for want of vacancies at 10th,20th& 30thyears of service.  
(xii) In order to provide better healthcare facilities to Officers and Jawans of CAPFs, “Ayushman 
CAPF” scheme has been launched in association with National Health Authority (NHA).

 Bureau of Immigration (BOI) 
 
4.9.9 In response to the query on the status of Marine Immigration check posts in India, the 
Ministry informed the Committee that at present there are 31 authorized Seaport Immigration 
Check Posts (ICPs) in the country out of which Immigration of 10 ICPs are under direct control of 
Bureau of Immigration (BOI), MHA and the remaining ICPs are manned by State Police personnel. 
Government of India has been promoting cruise operations through major Indian seaports. Though 
focus has been on facilitating foreign tourists, adequate matching efforts have not been made by the 
Port Trust authorities concerned to provide basic minimum facilities for professional Immigration 
services to the tourists inspite of the issue having been repeatedly taken up by BOI. 
 
4.9.10 Cochin seaport has been attracting cruise vessels since 2001 and the number of cruise 
vessels calling at the ports increased tremendously (2001=10 vessels, 2018=49 vessels). Similarly 
cruise traffic is expected to increase at all Seaports. There are difficulties in berthing ve ssels having 
length over 260 metres. Moreover, there are no infrastructure facilities available to handle the 
traffic of large vessels at Ernakulum wharf. Immigration authorities are expected to work in 
temporary structures/'Shamianas' set up by the Port Trusts, at the cost of the health of officials 
deployed there while exposing technical gadgets to inclement weather. BOI requires closed climate 
controlled environment along with leased line connectivity to conduct its operations. 
 

50 
 
4.9.11 At some ports, the foreign crews disembarking from the ships have to be taken outside the 
docks' secured areas without Immigration clearance. This is an undesirable situation. Every 
foreigner, upon arrival, as per security protocols is required to go through Immigration first as per 
procedure through access controlled counters. The offices of Immigration at many Seaports are 
however in dilapidated conditions. Though it was agreed upon to shift the office of Chennai 
Seaport to the Cruise buildings closer to the Immigration counters, however no action has been 
taken as yet. This temporary set up for Immigration creates difficulties for the transportation of 
technical gadgets, installation of the systems and programming etc. Due to lack of network cables 
and connectivity, it is difficult to use the makeshift counters for processing e-landing cards and 
passenger clearance inside the terminal and in the gangway. 
 
 4.9.12 It was further informed that the Seaport ICPs namely JNPT Mumbai, Mumbai Seaport, 
Kolkata, Vizhinjam, Vallarpadam, Cochin, Calicut, Chennai Mormugao & New Mangalore have 
inadequate infrastructure in terms of space/building for smooth Immigration function. Further, 
Immigration functions are carried out using ICT Technology which requires secure network 
connectivity through leased circuits and various Technical equipments viz. Servers, Computers, 
Passport Reading Machines, Barcode Readers etc. The ICT infrastructure requires appropriate 
housing in a Server Room with AC environment for proper functioning. The LAN (Local Area 
Networks) with Immigration Server Room and Immigration counter has to be properly laid out for 
smooth functioning. It is imperative that appropriate housing and infrastructure are made available 
for technical set up of Immigration infrastructure. 
 
4.9.13 The condition of the other 21 Seaport ICPs which are manned by the State Govt. personnel 
is even worse than the BOI controlled ICPs. Though BOI has supplied the required technical items 
e.g. computers, PRMs, Webcams etc. at these Seaports ICPs, the space and infrastructure provided 
to the Immigration authorities is grossly inadequate. 
 
4.9.14 Further, in recent past there have been strong pressure by Port Trusts and Tour Operators on 
BOI to perform Immigration function at berths, where no leased line connectivity exists, which is 
non-negotiable as without data flow from main server located at Delhi, no security vetting and 
immigration clearance can be done. 
 
4.9.15 While the airport sector has largely upgraded its infrastructure leading to smoother and 
faster immigration clearance and average traffic growth is of 8-10%, the Ports have not ke pt pace 
with the infrastructure requirements in the face of potential traffic growth. The Shipping industry 
i.e. the Ship Agents/Tour operators are stakeholders just like airlines and they need to invest in 
infrastructure development. Earlier, Ports were charging uniform tariff as decided by Tariff 
Authority for major ports on the basis of GRT of the vessels. However, now there is no uniformity 
of tariff charged at some Ports. 
 
4.9.16 The attention of Ministry of Port, Shipping and Waterways attention has been drawn to the 
infrastructure situation of these 31 sea-ports. There is an urgent need to plug the infrastructure gaps.  
 
4.9.17 The Committee notes that no significant improvement has been made in cre ation of 
adequate infrastructure at the Marine Immigration Posts. The Committee is astonished to 
note that the majority of the Marine Immigration Posts lack basic infrastructure facilities like 
building space, electricity/water connections, monitoring screens, canopy, etc. The Com mittee 
is aware that Bureau of Immigration requires closed climate controlled environment along 
with leased line connectivity to conduct its operations. But in some places, Immigration 
Authorities are working in temporary structures and putting health of officials deployed 
there at risk as also exposing technical gadgets to inclement weather.  

51

4.15.4 The following modifications have been made in the sub-scheme to rectify the shortcomings 
of the previous Scheme: 
 
i. Under this sub- scheme, central assistance has been continued to be provided to all the State 
Governments for weapons, megacity policing and equipment for Forensics, Information 
Technology, Communication, Training, etc. However, to facilitate targeted interventions, 
the earlier scheme was modified so as and activities of „mobility‟ and „construction of 
police infrastructure including housing‟ hav e been allowed for specific theatres viz. Jammu 
& Kashmir (which was covered under the scheme till 31th October, 2019), insurgency 
affected areas of North East(NE) Region and Left Wing Extremism(LWE) affected areas. 
Further, the items under „mobility‟ head  would be used only for strengthening field level 
police offices and not state level police offices. Ceiling of 25% on mobility was also 
introduced. 
  
ii. 20% of the allocation are to be awarded to States based on their performance in the police 
reforms  agenda decided for the year. Earlier there was no such provision.  
 
iii. Calendar for approval of the SAPs have been advanced so that these Plans are approved 
before commencement of the relevant financial year. 

57 
 
 
iv. States have been asked to submit State Security Plan (SSP) based on perspective/strategic 
planning. On the basis of SSP, SAPs are to be formulated.  
v. Process to allow modification up to 25% of total SAP size was simplified. 
 
vi. The mandatory earmarking of funds for procurement from OFB has been omitted 
 
The Committee was informed that the  General Financial Rules 2017 mandates, inter alia 
that before releasing funds to the State Governments under this scheme, it must be ensured 
that they have the capacity to actually spend the balance from the previous year and releases 
made during the current year. As substantial funds were unspent with the States‟ 
implementing agencies, no funds out of allocation at BE stage could be released. This 
financial discipline has specifically become necessary in view of the economic impact of 
COVID-19 global pandemic. Therefore, the following measures have been taken from time 
to time to enhance     utilisation of funds by the States- 
 
(i) „Better performance incentives‟ are awarded to States based on full utilisation of funds. 
Funds remaining unutilized by States are pooled together and distributed to the better 
performing States. This acts as a strong incentive to the States for faster utilization of funds. 
States which have performed better have received funds multiple times their allocation. 
 
(ii) Approval cycle has been advanced so that HPC approved SAPs are available to States much 
before the commencement of financial year. This has a positive effect on procurement cycle. 
Now states have more time to implement projects and submit utilisation certificates. In 
2019-20, fund was released to States in the month of April, 2019 itself; much earlier than 
previous years. 
 
(iii) State Level Empowered Committee (SLEC) has been reconstituted with the State Home 
Secretary heading the Committee in place of Chief Secretary earlier thereby saving  time for 
approval of proposals at State level. On account of any reason, if the State wants change of 
items approved in annual State Action Plan, approval in this regard is how given at the level 
of Chairman of High Powered Committee itself rather than approval of the HPC. This 
reduces time required for such modification resulting in early utilisation of funds. 
 
(iv) States have now prepared long term State Security Plans (3 to 5 years) keeping in mind 
their challenges and requirements. Due to this exercise it is easy for states to chalk out their 
annual actions plans. 
 
(v) In the meetings of High Powered Committee, States have been advised from time to time 
that for the procurement of BP Jacket, various weapons etc., the State Police may tag its 
requirements with ongoing procurement of the CAPFs. This achieves economy of scale as 
well as efficiency of procurements. This is especially beneficial in case of Police Forces of 
smaller States. 
 
The following measures have been taken to provide modern equipment for State police 
forces: 
 
(i) „Police‟ and  „Public Order‟ are State subjects  under the seventh Schedule to the 
Constitution of India. Modernization of police forces is a continuous and ongoing process. 
However, the Government of India supplements the efforts of the State Governments 

58 
 
towards equipping and modernizing of their police forces, under the scheme of „Assistance 
to States for Modernisation of Police‟ [erstwhi le scheme of Modernisation of Police Forces 
(MPF)]. Under this scheme, State Governments are provided central assistance for 
acquiring advanced weaponry such as Assault Rifles, all types of surveillance equipment 
including Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), Night Vision Devices (NVDs), CCTV 
surveillance systems and body worn camera systems, modern communication equipment 
and state-of-the-art equipment for Intelligence branches &forensic science laboratories. 
(ii) Under the scheme of Assistance to States for Modernisation of Police (ASMP), the State 
Governments formulate State Action Plan (SAPs) as per their requirements/strategic 
priorities, High Powered Committee approves these proposals. The HPC, which is chaired 
by Divisional Head of Police Modernisation Division and representatives of Financial 
Adviser (Home) and Director General, Bureau of Police Research and Development 
(BPR&D) as members. The Committee is also assisted by experts/resource persons from 
various Central level bodies such as Directorate of Forensic Science Services (DFSS), 
Directorate of Coordination Police Communication (DCPW), National Security Guard 
(NSG), Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) etc. 
Therefore, although flexibility of formulating SAPs has been provided to States, it is 
ensured that the States purchase appropriate items. 
(iii) BPR&D publishes compendium of equipment procured by State and UT Police Forces. 
Recently, BPR&D has published such Compendium for the period April, 2014 to March, 
2019. This also serves as reference document for all police forces. 
(iv) „Police‟ being State subject, the State police forces work under their respective State  
Governments. However, Ministry of Home Affairs has role of hand holding the State Police 
Forces on various common modernizations needs of these forces with guidance regarding 
appropriate technologies/equipments, apart from providing assistance to these Forces. 
Adoption of CAPFs‟ Qualitative Requirements & Trial Directives by  State Police Forces or 
circulation of SOPs in various areas of police functions are some of the examples of such 
knowledge sharing. This facilitates additional avenues of guidance for Police Forces, 
especially Police Forces of smaller States. This also avoids duplication of efforts and partly 
removes constraints emanating from the fact that „Police‟ and „Public  Order‟ are State 
subjects. 
(v) It has been experienced that different State Police Forces are at different levels of 
modernization in each of the components. Therefore, it is necessary to set a minimum 
essential benchmark in each of the components so as to bring the States which are lagging 
behind, to the minimum expected technological advancement. In this direction, MHA has 
circulated national standards in the field of forensics, K-9 & radio communication. 
 
4.15.5 Regarding under-utilization of funds by State Governments, the Committee was informed 
by the Home Secretary that at times even when States have  utilized the funds, there is dela yed 
submission of utilization certificates by them. Further, the utilization of funds by some States is 
also poor which is one of the reason for under-utilization of the funds under Modernisation of 
Police Forces.   
4.15.6 The Committee in the meeting of the Committee held on 16th February, 2021 sought to 
know the reasons for the use of body armour, big steel sticks and rods in place of lathis by Delhi 
Police in recent past. The Committee was of the view that it was not modernisation but regression 
and it was flashed across the country which is shocking.   The Home Secretary replied that the use 
of body armour, steel sticks etc. was purely a local level decision and there was no Government 
authorization even by senior officers of the Police Department of Delhi for the same.   

59 
 
4.15.7 The Committee observes that modernization of Police forces is the most urgent need of 
the hour. Therefore, it needs to be expeditiously taken up with a stipulated timeline. The  
Committee recommends that adequate funds must be allocated for purchasin g weaponry, 
bullet proof vehicles, jammers, bomb detection  equipments, communication gadge ts like 
wireless phones, etc., so that the Police personnel are well equipped to deal with the wor st 
situations like live mines on roads, etc. The Committee also recommends for stand ardization 
of Police vehicles all across the country as vehicles carry prestige for the Police. The 
Committee further recommends that the Ministry may ensure the availability of required 
funds as requested by the State Police Department without any procedural de lay of 
sanctioning of funds by the State Government to the Police Department. 
4.15.8 The Committee observes that providing adequate training is integral to modernization 
of Police forces. The Committee strongly believes that training programmes should focus on 
changing the mental attitude and sensitize Police personnel on various issues.  The Committee 
recommends that appropriate budgetary allocation should be made for training and 
sensitization of Police personnel. The Committee also recommends that it should be ensured 
that each and every Police personnel completes full training and under-training personnel 
particularly constables should not be posted for field duties for long. Special incentives may 
also be provided to rope in and attract quality trainers for Police personnel.

National Emergency Response System (NERS) and Cyber Crime Prevention against Women and  
Children (CCPWC).  The proposed expenditure out of the Nirbhaya Fund seeks to utilize the 
unspent balance lying at credit in the Fund. An amount of Rs.100 crore is proposed to be 
transferred to the Nirbhaya Fund in the Public Account in the year 2021-22. 
 
4.19.2 The Committee sought to know about the projects that are being implemented by MHA 
under the Nirbhaya Fund. The MHA replied that the projects for safety of women being 
implemented by Ministry of Home Affairs under the Nirbhaya Fund scheme include, 112 
Emergency Response Support System; providing one-time grant to States/UTs for Victim 
Compensation Fund; Cyber Crime Prevention against Women & Children; 3 projects for women 
safety by Delhi Police; Safe City projects in 8 Cities; Strengthening DNA analysis, cyber fo rensic 
& related facilities in State Forensic Sciences Laboratories; Setting up/ strengthening of Women 
Help Desks in Police Stations; Setting up/ strengthening of An ti-Human Trafficking Units in all 
districts; setting-up of a State-of-the-Art DNA  analysis facility in CFSL Chandigarh; Traini ng and 
Capacity Building of Criminal Justice functionaries.  
 
4.19.3 The Committee was informed by MHA that as per available information, there is a likely 
balance of  Rs. 1,167.91 crore in Nirbhaya Fund corpus in FY 2020-21, which would be available 
for Nirbhaya Fund projects in the FY 2021-22. In order to ensure optimum utilization of corpus 
reserves, the Nirbhaya Fund transfer proposed is Rs.100.00 crore. After taking into account the 
transfer of fund into the Nirbhaya Fund corpus from various Ministries, the projected demand for 
MHA projects under Nirbhaya Fund totaling to Rs. 759.59 crore in FY 2021-22 which could be 
met from the funds available in the corpus in the FY. 
 
4.19.4 A total of Rs. 321.15 crore had been utilized for the 112 National Emergency Response 

63 
 
System (ERSS) till the FY 2019-20, and the total utilization till 31 December 2020 was Rs. 336.52 
crore.  The single number 112 national emergency response service is now operational in 33 
States/UTs in the country and work is underway to complete the project in the remaining 3 States. 
 
4.19.5 The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) is implementing Cyber Crime Prevention for 
Women and Children (CCPWC) Scheme at an estimated cost of Rs. 223.198 Crore, to be met from 
Nirbhaya Funds of Ministry of Women & Children Development, for the implementation period 
2017-2020. The Scheme has been extended up to 31 st March, 2021. Further, implementation period 
of the scheme is being proposed to be extended for another two years beyond 31 st March, 2021. 
CIS Division has been able to utilize the funds to the extent of Rs. 112.62 crore up to the close of 
financial year 2019-20, out of the total cost provision of Rs.223.198 crore and the rest amount i.e 
Rs. 110.578 crore shall be utilized in the ensuing financial years 2020-21 to 2022-23.In Cyber 
Crime Prevention against Women and Children, a total of Rs.113.66 crore had been spent till FY 
2019-20 and as on December 2020, this has increased to Rs. 130.85 crore.  
4.19.6 For Strengthening of Forensic Science Laboratories, the Committee was informed that the 
Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2018 was enacted to, inter-alia, prescribe even more stringent 
penal provisions. While the law was made stringent, the Government also felt that effective 
deterrence lay not only in stringency of punishment but also in the delivery of the criminal justice. 
This required that the amendments effected in the law are backed up with adequate capacity 
building to ensure timeliness and efficiency in deliverance of criminal justice. In this regard, one 
of the measures which has been taken up is for strengthening DNA analysis, cyber forensic and 
related facilities in State Forensic Science Laboratories. Since „Police‟ and „Public order‟ are State 
subjects as per Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India, the Ministry undertook a gap analysis 
of the existing facilities through the States/UTs, and basis the demand assessment of each State/UT, 
has sanctioned projects in 20 States/UTs for total cost of Rs.189.45 crore. The remaining 
States/UTs are preparing their projects and the same are proposed to be taken up in the coming 
years. 
4.19.7 The Committee notes that the Ministry has sanctioned projects for strengthening DNA 
analysis, cyber forensic and related facilities in 20 States/UTs for total cost of Rs.189.45 crore. 
The Committee, recommends that the MHA may take up with the rem aining States for 
establishment of forensic and DNA analysis labs within a time frame and make  adequatory 
budgetary allocations for the same. This will help in improving investigating m achinery and 
strengthen criminal justice delivery mechanis m.

Cellular Jail  
5.2.3 The Committee sought to know about the steps taken to document the historiography of the 
freedom fighters who were imprisoned in Cellular Jail. The representative of UT of A&N Islands 
informed the Committee that the cellular jail also called Kala Paani was the land of no return many 
freedom fighters have suffered there.  While many of the freedom fighters have been documented, 
historiography definitely needs to look into various others who were kept in the cellular jail but 
went unnoticed.   
5.2.4 The Committee was further informed that the National Memorial Cellular Jail is a mute 
witness to the untold sufferings and sacrifices of our freedom fighters who laid down their lives for 
the cause of their motherland. A&N Administration, is committed to preserving India's heritage, so 
far the following actions has taken:- 
 
a. The Central Tower of the Cellular Jail has 18 marble plaques on the walls depicting the 
names of 513 freedom fighters incarcerated in the Cellular Jail from 1909-1938 . 
 
b. A Freedom Fighter‟s P hoto Gallery has been set up in the Administrative Block of the 
National Memorial Cellular Jail.The brief write-ups of revolutionary cases with available 
photographs of all Freedom Fighters incarcerated in the Cellular Jail are on display in the 
Gallery. 
 
c. The Department of Art & Culture, A&N Administration has made an effort to compile the 
brief profile of all freedom fighters in the form of a book “Unsung Heroes of Freedom 
Struggle in Andamans”- who were deported to the penal settlement in Andamans after the 
first war of independence in 1857 and revolutionary freedom fighters incarcerated in the 
Cellular Jail during 1909-1938. Necessary action is being taken to collect details of 
freedom fighters deported to the Cellular Jail from various State Archives. 
 
5.2.5 The Committee notes the efforts made by the Administration of UT of           A&N 
Islands for documentation of freedom fighters. The Committee recommend s that a 
biographical sketch may be created of all freedom fighters who were imprisoned  in cellula r 
jail during the course of freedom struggle so as to acquaint the incoming tourists of the 
history associated with the freedom struggle. 
Integration of tribals in the mainstream
 
 
5.2.6 Regarding the welfare of tribal population and plan of the UT administration to integrate 
them, the Committee was informed that interventions have been made to prolong the longevity of 
tribals and bring improvement in their health and basic things without forcing them. As a result, the 
population of Onges has gone up which was earlier dwindling down.  The Andaman and Nicobar 
Tribal Research and Training Institute (ANTRI) have submitted a proposal before the Tribal 
Welfare Ministry about the integration of tribals to the mainstream of development.     
5.2.7 There are six Scheduled Tribes i.e., the Andamanese, Onges, Jarawas, Sentinelese, Nicobarese 
and Shompens notified by the President of India under Article 342 (1) of the Indian Constitution vide  
the Constitution (Andaman & Nicobar Islands) Scheduled Tribes Order, dated 31 st March, 1959. Except 
Nicobarese the rest of the 05 tribes are categorized into Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs).  
 
5.2.8 The tribes of A&N Islands are in different stages of socio-economic condition. The Nicobarese 
have joined the mainstream and the Sentinlese are still in isolation practicing primordial hunting and 
gathering way of life.  The other tribes namely Jarawas, Onges, Andamanese and Shompens are partly 

70 
 
in contact with the outside population, but they prefer to remain in their own abode, particularly 
Shompens, Sentinelese and the Jarawas.

Aviation will benefit the Islander especially the weaker section while travelling on mainland-island 
sector at affordable fare. Further, due to operational limitations of the existing VSI Airport at Port

of the ecological sensitivity and strategic sensitivity of the region and is of the view that

distance from Tribune Chowk to the Chandigarh Airport was 2.71 km
.  Now, existing route from

(Mohali), which is causing difficulty to the residents of Chandigarh as they have to cover more 
distance and spend more  time to reach the Airport.  To cut short this road distance, certain options 
were proposed / deliberated, from time to time.  One of the options was to connect the old and ne w 
terminal through an underpass below the existing runway. This was not agreed to by the Air Force 
Authorities. In Chandigarh Master Plan (CMP) 2031, another proposal of road connectivity to

Punjab, so this needs to be done by Punjab Government.

International Airport is causing unnecessary inconvenience to the residents of Chandigarh as

the existing runway to make it convenient for the people travelling through the Chandigarh

5.4.7 The Committee was informed by the representative of UT of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and 
Daman and Diu that the UT came into existence on 26 th January, 2020 with the merger of erstwhile 
Union Territories of Dadra and Nagar Haveli, and Daman and Diu.  The Union Territory has taken 
steps for creation of physical and social infrastructure, Nand Ghars, health and wellness centres, e-
Aarogya implementation of Ayushman Bharat, Jampore beachfront road, etc. The work for civil 
terminal at Nani-Daman Coast Guard airport has already been awarded.  STP at Moti-Daman has 
already been established.  With regard to catamaran services, SCI has been approac hed and 
feasibility has been examined.  
5.4.8 The Committee was informed that to improve marine connectivity across the islands & 
mainland sector in Union Territory, U.T. Administration has decided to start Catamaran Ferry 
service between Daman & Diu to enable the citizens of the UT as well as tourists to travel from 
Daman & Diu through sea route.  
 
5.4.9 The Committee was informed by the representative of the UT that approval has been given 
for a medical college for 177 students in Silvassa which will enhance medical facilities in UT and 
provide an opportunity to local tribal students to pursue career in medicine.  E-Arogya, a paperless 
cloud-based healthcare service delivery system, has also been launched.  Recently, it has also been 
decided to privatize power infrastructure in the UTs for which bids have been invited. 
5.4.10 The Committee sought to know to know about the Bird Shelter in Jampore in Daman. The 
representative of the UT replied that Bird aviary project is in advanced stage of execution. 
Road connectivity in Badi Daman
 
 
5.4.11 The Committee was informed that the UT Administration of DNH & DD is an Industrial Hub & 
is developing in to a Tourist Destination. Due to such recent developments, the vehicular and tourist 
traffic have increased manifold, leading to vehicular traffic and industrial traffic congestion in the roads 
of Daman District. Therefore, as part of development & future planning, it has been envisaged to 
improve road connectivity in whole Daman District including Moti Daman. The Major road connecting 
Moti Daman is NH-848-B at Bamanpuja, (CH-KM 8/180), which in turn connects to National Highway 
NH-48 at Mohangam Fatak, Vapi (Gujarat). 
 
5.4.12 Total PWD roads in Daman district are 68.50 Km, (50.70 Km MDR & 17.80 Km ODR). Out of 
this, 24.50 Km have already been widened and re-carpeted and the remaining 44.00 Km MDR / ODR 
roads are proposed for strengthening, widening and re-carpeting in the F.Y 2021-2022. Out of this, 
16.00 Km of roads in Moti Daman have been widened and re-carpeted, and 5.00 Km road widening 

82 
 
from Dholar to Jampore up to Varliwad, Moti Daman is under progress. Moreover, all villages, 
settlements are connected with all weather roads in whole Daman District, including Moti Daman area. 
 
Airport expansion in Daman and Diu.
 
 
5.4.13 Presently an air-strip is available at Daman, which is under the control of Coast Guard Air 
Station, Daman. However, there is no Civil Terminal Building to cater to civil flights. Therefore, it was 
envisaged to develop a Civil Terminal Building in Daman as Daman & DNH is an industrial hub, 
wherein, Plastics, Pharmaceutical, Chemical & Chemical Products, Electrical & Electronics industries 
are concentrated. Also, this UT is a well-known tourist destination, where large number of tourists from 
neighboring states such as Gujarat, Maharashtra, and also from other states visit every year.  
 
5.4.14 Further, the Ministry of Civil Aviation, Government of India has awarded 04 routes to the UT 
Administration under Regional Connectivity Scheme UDAN 4.0., viz. (i) Vadodara-Diu-Vadodara (ii) 
Surat-Diu-Surat (iii) Daman-Diu-Daman and (iv) Ahmedabad-Daman-Ahmedabad. Therefore, as an 
interim measure the UT Administration has constructed a Temporary Civil Terminal with all basic 
facilities at the premise of Indian Coast Guard Air Station, Daman. Further, the Temporary Civil 
Terminal has been vetted by Airport Authority of India and Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BC AS). 
The flight operations are planned to commence on final certification from various agencies/ 
stakeholders involved. 
 
5.4.15 The Committee recommends that the MHA along with the UT Administration may 
construct bridges between Vanakbara and Kotda in Diu, Kalai and Jampore and Kolak and 
Nani Daman, both in Daman. 
5.4.16 The Committee notes that the area of Daman is 72 sq. kms which contains marshy 
land, funnel area, mangroves, rivers and the like.  Other than these areas, the remaining land 
available for development is only 22 sq. kms.  The area available in Diu is still less. Therefore,  
the Committee recommends that that entire Daman be declared under Coastal Regulation 
Zone II (CRZ II) instead of the existing Coastal Regulation Zone III (CRZ III) and Diu as an 
Island. The Committee also recommends that a ring road may be constructed in Daman , for 
which additional funds may be requested at RE stage. 
5.4.17 The Committee recommends that the MHA may take up with the Ministry of 
Railways for stoppage of the Mumbai New Delhi Rajdhani Express (12951/52)  at Vapi Station 
as it caters to the needs of Vapi, Silvassa, Daman and other nearby industrial town.  
5.4.18 The Committee notes that Dadra & Nagar Haveli predominantly is tribal area of the 
UT of  Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu. Therefore, the Committee recommends 
promotion and incentivisation of the arts and crafts of these tribal communities will help in 
generation of revenue and jobs for them. The Committee also recommends to give reservation 
to the residents of the UT for group C & D posts of various departments.

Under-utilization of funds
 
 
5.5.3 The Committee sought to know about the reasons for lower spending of budget in the UT for 
FY 2020-21. The Administration of UT of Ladakh informed the Committee that the reasons for 
savings of funds are as under: - 
(i) Enforcement of lockdown norms due to Covid-19 Pandemic. 
(ii) Working season lost in lockdown and unlock started in off season. 
(iii) Ladakh depends on labour coming from outside. Due to lock down, the execution of 
works was affected. As a result, the responses to the tenders were also affected.  
(iv) Being a new UT, capacity building exercise with relation to employees and implementing 
agencies including strengthening of system is being undertaken in a big way.  
(v) Big-ticket infrastructural projects require comprehensive planning and specialist 
consultants for preparing DPRs. There is also a requirement of designing the projects 
keeping in view energy efficiency and various other aspects related to the region. This 
requires thorough consultation with stakeholders and expert agencies.  
(vi) Various projects have been given to Central Public Sector Undertaking(s) like CPWD, 
NHIDCL and WAPCOS. They took time to establish their offices in the UT of Ladakh for 
planning/execution of projects entrusted to them.

(i) Constitution of requisite Contract Committees and Local Purchase Committees.

and Consultants for timely execution of various projects.

5.6.7 As islands are scattered in the Arabian Sea and isolated from the mainland, shipping sector 
is the lifeline of the islands. Out of total allocation of Rs.1,440.56 crore, 38% i.e. Rs.548.20 crore is 
exclusively for Transport sector (Port, Shipping and Aviation).  UTL Administration has already 
been operating passenger and cargo ships as well as High Speed Vessels for ensuring inter-isl and 
and mainland-island marine connectivity.  Acquisition of ships and vessels are in accordance to the 
15 years Perspective Plan 2015-2030, which is already approved by the Ministry. 
5.6.8 The Ministry of Civil Aviation has been requested to expand the connectivity across the 
islands, i.e., Agatti, Minicoy and Kavaratti, under UDAN Scheme and they have requested for 
seaplane service also across the island.  Further, a big Navy airport is coming up in Minicoy Island 
on the southern tip of Lakshadweep which  will transform the entire economy of that region.  The 
airstrip of the Agatti is being expanded for use of large planes to increase the carrying capacity of 
the planes which is about 60-70  persons per flight right now. The Airports Authority of India has 
also been asked to make feasibility study so that the Airbus 320 can also land at Agatti island. The 
Committee sought to know whether the UT of Lakshadweep  has helicopter services. The 
representative of UT of Lakshdweep replied that three Pawan Hans helicopters are being used  for 
medical evacuation only and till now no private operators have come in the UT for heli-tourism. 
5.6.9 The Committee is of the view that turboprops aircrafts with 40-70 seating capacity 
require very short take-off and landing strips and are economically viable. As such, they ar e 
ideally suited for the islands and there is no need to land heavy aircrafts and airbuses in the 
Islands.  Therefore, the focus should be on optimal use of the small aircrafts with STOL 
(short takeoff and landing) to promote tourism.  The Committee recommends to revisit the 
proposal for extension of runway for landing Airbus as it is not economically viable and in the 
ecologically sensitive areas it may not be advisable. The Committee also recommend s to take 
appropriate steps for attracting private operators for heli-tourism as it will help tourist  to 
move swiftly from one island to other and also enjoy the aerial view of beautiful land scape of 
the islands.

5.6.10 The Committee was informed by the representative of MHA that the Government

5.6.11 The Committee was informed by the Administration of UT of Lakshdweep, that considering

100% project target upon commissioning, it has become necessary to incorporate marine and 
shipping expertise at every stage of the project, such as identification of site, model studies, 
preparation of DPR and implementation etc. It has also become necessary to have a separate  
establishment for Lakshadweep headed by a Chief Engineer with complete administrative and 
financial powers for implementation of harbor development projects and timely maintenance o f 
harbor infrastructure. 
5.6.12 The Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways has been requested to establish a separate 
Division of Andaman and Lakshadweep Harbour Works (ALHW), a subordinate organization of 
Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, to be headed by a Chief Engineer with complete 
administrative and financial powers and also involvement of Marine and Shipping 
expertise/consultancy for gaining efficiency in harbor development and maintenance in 
Lakshadweep.  The Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways has constituted a Committee  to 
decide the modalities for distribution of manpower, budget and other issues likely to arise in case of 
bifurcation of ALHW.  Based on recommendations of the Committee, further action on 
restructuring of ALHW will be considered by Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways. 
5.6.13 The Committee is of the view that the passenger ship is the lifeline of the people of UT of 
Lakshdweep as connectivity to the island is very difficult. But, the Committee notes that there is no 
embarkation or disembarkation facility during night and passengers have to sleep in boats till 
morning.  The reason is the limited infrastructure.  There are six Islands out of which eastern side 
jetties have been made for four Islands  The reason for this persistent problem is  the absence of  
charge of Harbour Works Authority to the UT of Lakshadweep due to which, proper monitoring is 
not being done and infrastructure work is being  delayed for years.   
5.6.14 The Committee notes that the Administration of the UT of Lakshadweep does not 
have any control over the implementing agency of the Harbour Development. The Com mittee 
is of the view that that a separate Division of Andaman and Lakshadweep Harbour Works 
(ALHW) should be established for gaining efficiency in Harbour Development and 
maintenance in Lakshadweep. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the MHA may 
delegate control of the project to the Administration of the UT of Lakshadweep on a priority  
basis. This will ensure the role of UT Administrator in discharge of its duties and justify 
proper utilisation of funds allocated to the UT.

Fisheries 
 
5.6.24 The  total fisheries potential of UTL has been estimated at One Lakh metric tons by Central 
Marine Fishries Research Institute (CMFRI). However, the present exploitation /fish landing is 20-
25% of potential resources. To cope up with the changing standards of fishing industry and to 
exploit the deep sea resources, size of the crafts needs to be increased and the facilities on board are 
to be enhanced to carry out multiple day fishing operations. Proposal is to extend financial 
assistance for introduction of larger deep sea fishing vessels, up grading the existing crafts and to 
supply latest fish finding and navigation equipment for use on board the fishing vessels. The UT 
administration is implementing a Scheme “Strengthening of Fishing Fleets & Improvement of 
Crafts”. Under this scheme, department provides financial assistance of 40%  to the local poor 
fishermen  for the construction of  bigger type multi day pole & line/long line  fishing   vessels, 
medium type pole & line fishing  boats etc.  
 
5.6.25 Besides, encouragement is being provided to   fishermen for setting up of hatcheries and 
production of ornamentals under controlled conditions. The research institutes have developed 
technologies for the hatchery and grow-out of clown and damsel fishes. A sea weed cultivation 
project has already been initiated with coordination with CMFRI at Rs. 49 Lakhs earmarked for 
2020-21. 
 
5.6.26 For Development of Post-Harvest Fish Processing Facilities & Marketing, UTLA has 
proposed to create shore based infrastructural facilities like ice plants, cold storages etc. for the 
utilization of fish waste, a fish meal plant and production of value added fishery products. An 
integrated fish processing unit is also proposed and Rs. 35 Lakhs is earmarked for the purpose. In 
addition to this, an amount of Rs. 1 crore is earmarked  under capital head for purchase of 
equipment & machinery for Boat Building Yard, Workshop & slip way/ Ice Plant & Fish market 
etc.   
 
5.6.27 Marketing is the main issue faced by local fishermen. The Department of Fisheries is 
promoting marketing of fresh fish by facilitating bigger type collecting vessels for colle ction & 
transportation of fish from islands to mainland. Further, UTL Administration has taken a policy 
decision to open up the market to Marine Products Export Development Authority (MPEDA) 
registered exporters to collect and export Tuna and Tuna like fishes from island to mainland. For 
Sashmi Sea food, one of the MPEDA registered exporters has already set up a packing/ processing 
unit at Agatti. Moreover, the Dept. of Fisheries, UTL has signed a MoU with Kerala State Coastal 
Area Development Corporation (KSCADC) for handholding  in post harvest and marketing of 
fishes especially Tuna. The draft agreement with MPEDA for the purpose of technical 
collaboration for exporting of Tuna and other fisheries products has also been finalized and the 
same will be signed within one month. 
 
5.6.28 The Committee observes that the fishing potential of the UT of Lakshdweep is n ot 
being harnessed properly. The fishermen are not catching enough fish  due  to lack of 
infrastructure like small crafts, ice plant, cold storage, processing units, etc. to catch, preserve 
and process fishes before they are sold in the market. The Committee is of the view that  
proper storage and processing unit will give fishermen the confidence that if the c atch is not 
sold, at least it can be preserved, and can be sold in the market the next day. T he Committee, 
therefore, recommends that investments should be made for creation of basic inf rastructure 
to boost fishing industry in the UT to provide income security to the fishermen. The
