1.7 Central Pool of Resources for NER 
 
1.7.1 In 1997-98, when it was found that the actual expenditure of Ministries/Departments for 
NER was less than the mandatory ceiling of 10 per cent, the Government decided to create a 
"Central Resource Pool" into which the unutilized portion of the 10 per cent earmarked GBS 
would accrue at the end of the financial year.  Since 1998-99, the annual surrendered amounts 
out of the earmarked outlays of all the non -exempted Central Ministries/Departments for NER 
have been accounted as accruals to this Pool and the annual expenditure of the Ministry under 
the NLCPR scheme is bei ng accounted as withdrawal from the Pool. However, this is a notional 
pool, maintained on a proforma basis by the Ministry of Finance. The Ministry of DoNER 
monitors Ministry -wise expenditure/ surrendered amounts for the purpose of ascertaining the 
accrual to the NLCPR pool in consultation with the Ministry of Finance. 
 
INSTITUTIONS UNDER MINISTRY OF DoNER 
 
1.8 North Eastern Council (NEC) 
 
1.8.1 The North Eastern Council (NEC) was constituted as a statutory advisory body by an Act 
of Parliament under the NE C Act, 1971 (84 of 1971) marking the beginning of a new chapter of 
concerted and planned endeavour for rapid socio -economic development of the North Easter n 
Region (NER). Over the last 48 years, the Council has played a significant role in ushering 
development into the Region at a time when most States were in their formative stages. Road and 
air connectivity were supported, foundations for important regional Institutions were established, 
and various socio -economic infrastructures were created across the length and breadth of the 
Region, making a difference in the lives of the people and thereby earning goodwill in the local 
community. Presently, NEC is looking to continue its efforts, especially in terms of gap-filling in 
areas which have escaped the attention of various development agencies and creating 
convergence at different levels. NEC is also looking at building capacities, sharing best practices 
and introducing cutting-edge technologies among the NE States. 
 
1.9 North East Cane and Bamboo Development Council (NECBDC)  
 
1.9.1 Cane and Bamboo Technology Centre (CBTC) now re -named as North East Cane and 
Bamboo Development Council (NECBDC) is an ISO 9001:20 08 certified organization and was 
established in the year 2000 as part of Cane and Bamboo Technological Upgradation and 

6 
 
Networking Programme of United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), where the 
Department of Science & Technology (DST), Govt. of India and United Nations Industrial 
Development Organization (UNIDO) were the main stakeholders. CBTC has been registered as a 
Society on 21 st July, 2004 with Secretary NEC as Chairman. CBTC has been determined and 
committed to work to develop the cane and bambo o sector in the country, especially in the NE 
Region. 
 
1.10 North Eastern Handicrafts and Handlooms Development Corporation Limited  
(NEHHDC) 
 
1.10.1 The North Eastern Handicrafts and Handlooms Development Corporation Ltd 
(NEHHDC) was established in the year 1977 at Shillong, Meghalaya with the mandate of 
promotion and development of Handlooms and Handicrafts Sector in the North Eastern Region. 
NEHHDC h as been providing marketing support through procurement of Handicrafts and 
Handlooms products directly from the Artisans, Weavers and Self -Help Groups at clusters and 
selling the same through its Sales Emporia located at Shillong, Guwahati, Kolkata, New De lhi 
and Gujarat and through Sales Promotion Offices located at Chennai and Bangalore and also 
through the conduct of various exhibitions and marketing events all over the country. 
 
1.11 North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation Limited  
(NERAMAC)  
 
1.11.1 North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation (NERAMAC) Limited was 
incorporated in 1982 as a Central Public Sector Enterprise under the administrative control of the 
Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region (DoNER). NERAMAC has been envisaged 
and is functioning as not just a marketing agency for farmers and entrepreneurs, but also 
undertakes agri-horti projects, skill curriculum supplies inputs, GI produ ces promotion activities, 
agri-events and assists in setting up of horticulture value chain (food processing) etc. to approach 
the aspect of Agri -Horti development holistically. A revival package for NERAMAC was 
approved in August 2021. The Corporation is on track to achieve a turnover target of ₹ 64 crores 
set at the time of approval. 
 
Livelihood & Entrepreneurship

1.12.1 The North Eastern Region Community Resource Management Society (NERCRMS) is a 
society under the North Eastern Council (NEC), Ministry of DoNER, Government of India for 
the implementation of development projects in the North Eastern Region of India. The Soc iety 
successfully implemented 3 (three) phases of the NERCORMP project  i.e. (a) NERCORMP -I 
from 1999 to 2008 jointly funded by Govt. of India and IFAD’ (b) NERCORMP -II from 2010 to 
2017 jointly funded by Govt. of India and IFAD and (c) NERCORMP -III from 2 014 to 2021 
with funding from Govt. of India only.  
 
1.12.2 The NERCORMP-I & II was implemented in 6 districts in States i.e. Karbi Anglong and  
Dima Hasao districts of Assam; Ukhrul and Senapati districts of Manipur;  West Garo Hills and 
West Khasi Hills districts of Meghalaya. The NERCORMP -III was implemented in Changlang 

7 
 
and Tirap (including Logding) districts of Arunachal Pradesh, Chandel and Churachandpur 
districts of Manipur. The society developed community -based institutions for implementation of 
NERCORMP-I, II & III.  During three phases of NERCORMP , the society formed 2889 Natural 
Resource Management Groups (NaRM -Gs), 8403 Self Help Groups (SHGs), 290 NaRM -G 
Cluster Associations, 300 SHG Federations, 4 Community -Based Micro Credit Institutions and 
50 Farmer Producer Groups. A total 1,18,843 Household in 2532 villages benefited from 
NERCORMP I, II & III with a total cost to Govt. of India ₹ 731.28 crores (Total investment 
including funds from other agencies, support from financial institutions and com munity 
contribution was ₹ 970.94 crores).  
 
1.12.3 The NERCRMS continue implementing development interventions beyond NERCORMP 
covering all 8 (eight) States of NER of India with sanction/allotment of additional 
projects/schemes of North Eastern Council beyond 2021. 
 
1.13 North Eastern Development Finance Corporation Ltd. (NEDFi) 
 
1.13.1 North Eastern Development Finance Corporation Ltd (NEDFi) is a public limited 
company established in 1995 under the Companies Act 1956. It is notified as a Public Financial 
Institution under Section 4A of the said Act and is registered as a Non -Banking Financial 
Company (NBFC) in 2002 with RBI. The core business of the Corporation comprises lending 
activities (fund -based) and fee -based activities. The lending activities are u ndertaken through  
project finance schemes and microfinance schemes. The Corporation also provides fee -based 
Advisory & Consultancy Services to the Central and State Governments. 
 
1.13.2 NEDFi has been playing an important role in facilitating the setting u p of new industrial 
and service sector projects in the North Eastern States. During 1st January to 31 st December, 
2022, NEDFi extended financial assistance to 3263 projects with total sanctions & disbursements 
of ₹  1035.34 crores and ₹  725.34 crores respectively, facilitating the capital formation of ₹  
2119.64 crores. Various sectors financed were hotels & tourism, healthcare, education & training 
institute, food processing, handlooms & handicrafts, microfinance etc.  
 
1.14 Science & Technology Intervention North Eastern Region (STINER) 
 
1.14.1 Ministry of DoNER with the close collaboration of the office of the Principal Scientific 
Adviser (PSA) to the Government of India initiated STINER ( Science & Technology 
Interventions in the North East Region ) in 2017 -18 as a mechanism for synergy between 
technology and users. STINER supports appropriate technology dissemination of field -tested 
technologies from S&T institutions to the farmers /artisans of NER which helps augment 
economic development/livelihood in the NER. The STINER Project was officially transferred to 
North Eastern Council, Shillong from Ministry along with a budget Provision of ₹ 40 crores in 
June, 2016 for sanctioning funds to implement the project by CSIR -NEIST, Jorhat. STINER has 
been proposed to be implemented in Hub & Spoke mode, where STINER-hub is started at CSIR-
NEIST, Jorhat and a STINER -spoke is to be established at every North E astern States. Already, 
STINER-Spoke at SASARD, Nagaland has been established and six other STINER spoke s 
projects for the State of Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Manipur, Tripura and Sikkim 
have been submitted, presented, reviewed and waiting for final approval.

2.3.4 The Ministry in the Committee’s meeting on 27 th February, 2023  informed that Budget 
Outlay allocated at the RE stage in 2021 -22 has been fully utilized.  However, the progress of 
expenditure in the year 2022-23 is around 16%, with three months of the current financial year still

NERSDS-Programme, Special Development Packages viz. BTC, KAATC  and DHATC witnessed 
under-utilization of funds due to implementation of the revised procedure for the flow of funds in 
compliance with the Department of Economic Affairs OM dated 09th March, 2022.

2.3.5 The Committee was informed that there has been a substantial change in the way of  
allocation and spending of funds in the FY 2022 -23. Previously, the funds were released to the 
States or their working institutions in advance installments from the budget al location and were 
considered as expenditure. This used to lead to actual spending later, which the Ministry used to 
know through certificates after utilization. The next time, funds were again sanctioned in advance. 
Further, funds were released via Treasury to State Governments / Implementing Agencies (IAs). 
According to the revised procedure for the flow of funds implemented in accordance with the 
Department of Economic Affairs OM dated March 9, 2022, funds are released to Implementing 
Agencies (IAs) by CNA against submitted bills for work done by IA s. Now, funds  can only be 
released to an IA after they submit a “Zero Balance Certificate”. The Committee was also 
informed that NEDFi has been selected as the Central Nodal Agency (CNA) by the Ministry o f 
DoNER and has opened scheme-wise accounts for implementing the said guidelines.  
 
2.3.6 The Committee was informed that since this was the first year of the implementation of the 
new system, the Ministry had to decide whether the funds released earlier to the States or their 
working institutions as advances were still unspent  or for which a  utilization certificate ha d not 
been given.  So, either a utilization certificate is to be given to confirm that the funds have been 
spent or to be returned to the scheme -wise accounts created by the CNA. This process is going on 
right now. It was further informed that the unspent balances availab le with the State 
Governments/Implementing Agencies were required to be returned to CNA Accounts.  
 
2.3.7 According to Ministry’s provisional estimate, as of April 1, 2022, States had about ₹ 3,200 
crores against donor schemes whose utilization certificate s had not been received, and it was not 
known whether they were spent or not. Further, out of this amount of about ₹ 3,200 crores, 
utilization certificates worth about ₹ 1,900 crores have been given by the States that this amount 
has been spent, and about ₹ 800 crores have been deposited in CNA accounts. They will be made 
available to them again when they spend in the future. For the remaining ₹ 500 crores, some States 
are still returning or giving utilization certificates. For this, the deadline for this year has been set 
as March, 2023. The Ministry is in constant touch with them and monitoring this. 
 
Observation/ Recommendation 
 
2.3.8 The Committee notes that, in accordance with the Department of Economic Affairs' 
directives, a revamped mechanism for transferring funds under Central Sector Schemes 
has been implemented. The Committee also notes that the Ministry has been able to utilize 
around 16% of the allocated amount in the first three quarters of the financial year. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry may strengthen its coordination 
mechanism with the NEC, States and implementing agencies so that such a situation , that 
arose in the Financial Year 2022-23, can be addressed promptly and without delay in order 
to maximize the utilization of funds.  The Committee also recommends that the Ministry 
make all-out efforts to ensure that the balance of ₹  500 crores is accounted for by the close 
of the financial year 2022-23.

CENTRAL SECTOR SCHEMES 
 
3.1 Schemes of North East Council  
 
3.1.1 The North Eastern Council, which was constituted as a statutory advisory body by an Act 
of Parliament under the North Eastern Council Act, 1971 (Act No. 84 of 1971) , works under the 
administrative control of the Ministry of DoNER. It provides financial assistance for various 
projects, including infrastructure projects like the construction of roads, improving air 
connectivity, etc., through State Governments.   
 
3.1.2 The "Schemes of the NEC" is a Central Sector Scheme with a 100% Grant from the 
Government of India. The projects under the scheme are implemented in focused areas through 
designated agencies of the States/Central Government with a stipulation that in the case of State 
agencies, the funds will be transferred to implementing agencies.  
 
3.1.3 The Committee was informed that the Union Cabinet, in its meeting held in January 
2020, approved earmarking of 30 per cent of the North E astern Council's (NEC's) allocation for

3.2.1 The Scheme of ‘Central Pool of Resources for North East and Sikkim’ is conventionally

assistance to the projects prioritized by the Central and State Government. The Ministry gets 
annual budgetary allocation for funding projects under NLCPR Scheme. Funding of projects 
under the NLCPR scheme is on a 90:10 sharing pattern betwe en Central and State Governments.

financial assistance to NER States is provided to fill up the gaps in specified sectors of :- 
 
(a) physical infrastructure relating to water supply, power and connectivity to enhance 
tourism and  
(b) social sectors for the creation of infrastructure in the areas of primary and secondary 
sectors of education and health.

3.4 Special package for Bodoland Territorial Council (BTC) 
  
3.4.1 A Memorandum of Settlement (MoS) was signed between the Government of India, the 
Government of Assam and Bodo Liberation Tigers (BLT) on 10 th February, 2003, with the 
objective of creating an autonomous self -governing body – the Bod oland Territorial 
Council (BTC) within the State of  Assam under the Sixth  Schedule to the  Constitution of India. 
The BTC was essential for fulfilling economic, educational and linguistic aspirations, preserving 
the socio-cultural and ethnic identity of the  Bodos and for development in the BTC area. The 
said MoS inter alia envisaged an additional Development Package for BTC to accelerate the 
development of the area and to meet the aspirations of the people.   
 
3.4.2 The Ministry stated that under this packag e, the Government of India agreed to provide 
financial assistance of ₹ 100 crores per annum for 5 years (₹ 500 crores) for projects to develop 
Socio-Economic infrastructure in BTC areas over and above Normal Plan Assistance to Assam. 
An additional BTC Package of ₹ 250 crores was announced by the Prime Minister in August 
2008, and this enhanced the total outlay to the tune of ₹ 750 crores (₹ 500 crores + ₹ 250 crores). 
Accordingly, 65 projects at an approved cost of ₹ 749.63 crores have been sanctioned, and an 
amount of ₹ 720.66 crores has been released.  Out of these 65 projects, 54 projects with an 
approved cost of ₹ 589.11 crores have been completed. 
 
3.4.3 A new Memorandum of Settlement (MoS) has been signed by the Government of India, 
the Government of Assam and Bodo Groups (ABSU and NDFB factions) on 27 th January, 2020. 
As per clause 10.1 of MoS dated 27 th January, 2020, the Government of Assam, may earmark a 
sum of ₹ 250 crores per annum for a period of three years for the development of the area under 
BTC. Further, the Government of India may contribute an additional amount of ₹  250 crores per 
annum for the same period.   
 
3.4.4 Explaining the reason for the significant enhancement of allocation from ₹ 30.00 crores 
in BE 2022-23 to ₹ 100.00 crores in BE 2023-24, the Ministry informed that the allocated funds 
will be utilized toward the comm itted liabilities against the ongoing projects, which is around ₹  
20 crores, and the projects identified for sanction under new special development package for 
BTC.

3.7 Prime Minister’s Development Initiative for North East Region (PM-DevINE) 
 
3.7.1 PM-DevINE was announced in the Union Budget 2022 -23 as a new Scheme to address 
development gaps in the North Eastern Region (NER). The parameters of NE States regarding 
Basic Minimum Services (BMS) are below the national average, and there are critical 
development gaps as per the NER District Sustainable D evelopment Goal (SDG) Index 2021 -22 
prepared by NITI Aayog, UNDP and MDoNER.  PM-DevINE was announced to address these 
BMS shortfalls and development gaps. It is a Central Sector Scheme with 100% Central funding 
and has an outlay of ₹ 6,600 crores for 4 years from 2022-23 to 2025-26 (remaining years of the 

25 
 
15th Finance Commission period). It is in addition to the quantum of resources available for the 
development of the NER. It will not be a substitute for existing Central and State Schemes.  
 
3.7.2 The objectives of PM-DevINE are to:  
(i) Fund infrastructure convergently, in the spirit of PM GatiShakti;  
(ii) Support social development projects based on the felt needs of the NER;  
(iii) Enable livelihood activities for youth and women;  
(iv) Fill the development gaps in various sectors. 
 
3.7.3 The Ministry informed the Committee that PM-DevINE will lead to the creation of 
infrastructure, support industries, and social development projects and create livelihood activities 
for youth and women, thus leading to  income and employment generation . It will provide 
support to infrastructure and social development projects which may be larger in size and will 
also provide an end–to-end development solution instead of isolated projects.  
 
3.7.4 The Ministry informed that efforts will be made to complete the PM-DevINE projects by 
2025-26 so that there are no committed liabilities beyond that year. It will be implemented 
through the North Eastern Council, Central Ministries/ agencies or State Government agencies. 
Measures would be taken to ensure adequate operation and maintenance of the projects 
sanctioned under PM-DevINE so that they are sustainable. To limit construction risks of time 
and cost overrun falling on the Government, projects would be implemented on Engineeri ng-
Procurement-Construction (EPC) basis, to the extent possible. 
 
3.7.5   Eleven projects costing about ₹  1500 crores, including the seven projects announced in

CHAPTER – IV 
 
SCHEMES, POLICIES AND PROGRAMMES 
 
4.1 Agriculture and Allied Sectors  
 
4.1.1 The Committee was informed by the Ministry that the Department of Agriculture and 
Farmers welfare ( DA&FW) is organized into 28 Divisions for coordination with State-level 
agencies and implementation of schemes in their respective fields. Further, one Public Sector 
Undertakings (National Seeds Corporation), nine autonomous bodies including Small Farmers’ 
Agri Business Consortium, National Horticulture Board, Natio nal Centre for Cold Chain 
Development etc., ten national level cooperative organizations and two authorities are 
functioning under the administrative control of the Department. Most of the central sector’s 
schemes related to Agriculture are implemented by DA&FW including Agriculture Infrastructure 
Fund, Mission Organic Value Chain Development for North Eastern Region (MOVCDNER) etc.       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               
4.1.2 The major Schemes implemented by DA&FW to develop agriculture and farmers’ 
welfare in NER include:  
 
a) Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi  
The Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi (PM Kisan) is a central sector scheme under 
which financial support o f ₹ 6,000 per year in three equal instalments is transferred directly into 
the bank accounts of eligible farmers under Direct Benefit Transfer. The scheme became 
operational in December 2018. Under the scheme, State Government and UT administration 
identify the farmer families which are eligible for financial support as per the scheme guidelines.  
 
b) Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana 
The Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) provides insurance coverage and 
financial support to the farmers in the event of fa ilure of any of the notified crops due to natural 
calamities, pests & diseases. The scheme also encourages farmers to adopt innovative and 
modern agricultural practices and stabilizes the income of farmers to ensure their continuance in 
farming activity. T he scheme is implemented by a multiagency framework by a few selected 
insurance companies under the supervision of the Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare 
(MoA&FW), Govt of India. 
 
c) Agriculture Infrastructure Fund 
The Agriculture Infrastructure Fund ( AIF) is a central sector scheme to facilitate the 
financing of agricultural infrastructure at the post -harvest stage i.e., farm gates and aggregation 
points.  The scheme was launched in 2020 and has a total outlay of ₹ 1 Lac crore. The scheme 
provides Interest subvention of 3% p.a., limited to ₹ 2 crores per project in one location, though 
the loan amount can be higher. The scheme also has a cap on lending rate, so that benefit of 
interest subsidy reaches the beneficiary and services to farmers remain affordable. 
 
d) Mission Organic Value Chain Development for North – Eastern Region 
The Mission Organic Value Chain Development for North Eas tern Region 
(MOVCDNER) is a sub mission under National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture (NMSA). It 
is a central sector scheme and aims at the development of certified organic production in a value 

31 
 
chain mode to link growers with consumers and to support the development of the entire value 
chain starting from inputs, seeds, and certification, to the creation of facilities for collection, 
aggregation, processing marketing and brand building initiative. 
 
e) Modified Interest Subvention Scheme 
The Government implements a modified interest subvention scheme to ensure that 
nominal interest rates are charged to farmers for short -term crop loans for agriculture and allied 
sectors. Under the scheme for FY 2021 -22, the lending rate to farmers and the rate of interest 
subvention has been kept at 7% and 2% respectively.  
 
f) Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana - Remunerative Approaches for Agriculture and 
Allied Sector Rejuvenation 
The scheme was originally initiated as RKVY in 2007 to ensure the holistic development 
of agriculture and allied sectors by allowing States to choose their own agriculture and allied 
sector activities as per the State Agriculture Plan. It is a central sponsored scheme with a funding 
pattern ratio of 60:40 between the Centre and States and 90:10 for North Eastern States and 
Himalayan States. RKVY -RAFTAAR aims to make farming a remunerative economic activity 
through the strength ening of farmer’s efforts, promoting Agri -business entrepreneurship, focus 
on pre & post-harvest infrastructure.  
 
g) Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture 
Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture (MIDH) is a Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme for the holistic growth of the horticulture sector covering fruits, vegetables, root & tuber 
crops, mushrooms, spices, flowers, aromatic plants, coconut, cashew, cocoa, and bamboo. Under 
MIDH, the Government of India (GOI) contributes 60% of the total outl ay for developmental 
programmes in all the States except States in North East and the Himalayas, 40% share is 
contributed by State Governments.  
 
4.1.3 The Committee, in its meeting held on 27th February, 2023, discussed about various 
indigenous crop varieties in the NER. The Committee discussed about Boka Saul; an indigenous 
variety of rice produced exclusively in lower regions of Assam. It was discussed that this rice is 
not cooked conventional ly, as it can be soaked in warm or cold water, and after around 30 -40 
minutes, it is ready for consumption. It does not need any kind of fuel to cook. The Committee 
believes that the potential of this variety of rice can be tapped as it is not only nutriti ous but can 
be used as an alternate source of food in emergencies like flood, earthquake and disaster 
management. It could also be used for army and armed forces personnel posted in high altitude 
or remote areas.  
 
4.1.4 Further, the abundance of Bamboo in  NER and the viability of bamboo for commercial 
purpose was also discussed in the meeting of the Committee. Bamboo is not covered in the 
category of a tree after the amendment made to Indian Forest Act, 1927, and there is no 
prohibition on growing or cutti ng bamboo even outside the forest areas. This makes it easier to 
use Bamboo commercially. 
 
 
 
 

32 
 
Observation/ Recommendation 
 
4.1.5 Agriculture is one of the major sources of livelihood for the people of North Eastern 
Region and assisting and encouraging the farmers to continue their farming activities 
through the implementation of various schemes like Rashriya Krishi Vikas Yojana, 
Mission Organic Value Chain Development for North Eastern Region (MOVCDNER) etc. 
give impetus to agricultural development and upli ftment of the farmers in North Eastern 
Region.  The Committee appreciates the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) 
which is providing insurance coverage and financial support to the farmers in the event of 
failure of any notified crops due to natural c alamities, pest and diseases. The scheme also 
encourages farmers to adopt innovative and modern agricultural practices.  The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry of DoNER should make efforts that such 
schemes have a wider reach in NER and that maximum be nefits are reaped out of these 
schemes by the farmers.  
 
4.1.6 Taking note of the uniqueness of Boka Saul rice, the Committee believes that the 
potential of this variety of rice can be tapped. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
special consideration may be given and efforts may be made to commercialize this special 
variety of rice and bolster its reach beyond the State of Assam. 
 
4.1.7 Similarly, considering the abundance of Bamboo in NER the Committee notes that 
its commercial viability has not been  fully tapped. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Ministry may facilitate carrying out research activities in collaboration with 
various organizations well versed in this subject like the Indian Plywood Industries 
Research & Training Institute ( IPIRTI), situated in Bengaluru. This will enable the 
Ministry and respective States to utilize the immense potential of abundantly grown 
Bamboo in NER.  
 
4.1.8 The Committee further recommends that research on other indigenous crop 
varieties, such as beetl e nut, jackfruit etc. that are abundantly grown in NER, may be 
explored for its use for the welfare of not only the people of the region but also other parts 
of the country.

Eastern Region (MOVCDNER) Scheme since 2015 -16 to promote certified organic production

building, brand promotion and contract production.

4.9 Kaladan Multi Modal Transit Transport (KMMTT) 
 
4.9.1 The Committee inquired about the status of the Kaladan Multi Modal Transit Transport 
(KMMTT). The Ministry informed the Committee that KMMTT, a strategic connectivity project 
to connect the eastern ports of India with Myanmar has two components: (i) Waterways 
component and (ii) Roadways component. 
(I)       Waterways component: The construction of port and inland water transport was 
completed in December 2018. All works for the operationalization of the port have been 
  completed. Sittwe port is now ready for operationalization. A trial run from Sittwe port 
(Myanmar) was conducted successfully on 13 January, 2023.  
(II)      Road component: The Road component of KMMTT includes a new green field road 
project of 109.2 km to be built from Paletwa in Myanmar to Zorinpui on the India -Myanmar 
border (Mizoram) to double -lane NH specifications. The work was earlier awarded to the Joint 
Venture (JV) of Engineers Projects (India) Limited and C&C Construction Co.  Ltd. in 2017. 
However, due to slow progress and the bankruptcy of the lead partner of JV, the contract was 
terminated. Now IRCON International has been appointed as the New Project Executing agency 
for the execution of the project. The agreement with IRCO N has been signed on 7 th March 2022. 
IRCON has awarded the contract for 40 km stretch from Paletwa end (Myanmar) i.e. 0 km –40 
km and for 99 km –109 km (from Zorinpui end). Work has started in 0 km –10 km section (i.e 
from Paletwa, Myanmar end). Surveying and site cleaning works have started in km 10 - km 40 
section (Myanmar end) and 99 km –109 km (Zorinpui, Mizoram end). 
 
Observation/ Recommendation 
 
4.9.2 The Committee appreciates the efforts made towards the completion of the 
waterways component of the Kaladan Multi Modal Transit Transport (KMMTT), a 
strategic connectivity project to connect the eastern ports of India with Myanmar, and all 
the works that have been done for the operationalization of the port. The Committee notes 
and hopes that since a new  Project Executing Agency has been appointed for execution of 
the road component of KMMTT, similar commitment may be shown to realise the 
completion of road component of the project in a time bound manner.

directives, a revamped mechanism for transferring funds under Central Sector Schemes

Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry may strengthen its coordination 
mechanism with the NEC, States and implementing agencies so that such a situation, that

through the implementation of various schemes like Rashriya Krishi Vikas Yojana, 
Mission Organic Value Chain Development for North Eastern Region (MOVCDNER) etc. 
give impetus to agricultural development and upliftment of the farme rs in North Eastern

failure of any notified crops due to natural calamities, pest and  diseases. The scheme also 
encourages farmers to adopt innovative and modern agricultural practices.  The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry of DoNER should make efforts that such 
schemes have a wider reach in NER and that maximum benefits are reaped o ut of these 
schemes by the farmers.  
 (Para 4.1.5) 
 
 Taking note of the uniqueness of Boka Saul rice, the Committee believes that the 
potential of this variety of rice can be tapped. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
special consideration may be gi ven and efforts may be made to commercialize this special 
variety of rice and bolster its reach beyond the State of Assam. 
 (Para 4.1.6) 
 
 Similarly, considering the abundance of Bamboo in NER the Committee notes that 
its commercial viability has not been fully tapped. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Ministry may facilitate carrying out research activities in collaboration with 
various organizations well versed in this subject like the Indian Plywood Industries 
Research & Training Institute (I PIRTI), situated in Bengaluru. This will enable the 
Ministry and respective States to utilize the immense potential of abundantly grown 
Bamboo in NER.  
 (Para 4.1.7) 
 
The Committee further recommends that research on other indigenous crop 
varieties, such a s beetle nut, jackfruit etc. that are abundantly grown in NER, may be 
explored for its use for the welfare of not only the people of the region but also other parts 
of the country. 
  (Para 4.1.8) 
 
 
 
 
Organic Farming in NER 

51 
 
 
The Committee notes that Sikkim has achieved the status of a fully organic farming 
state.  However, there is a need for dedicated machinery in NER looking into the capacity -
building mechanism of States and various agencies involved in agriculture and allied 
services towards strengthening  their organic farming infrastructure. The Committee 
recommends the Ministry of DoNER to provide its support and encouragement to other 
States of NER to achieve the status of an organic farming state. 
  (Para 4.2.5) 
Cold Storage facilities in NER 
 
The Comm ittee observes that,  out of 434  micro food processing enterprises in 
Assam with sanctioned loans under Prime Minister Formalization of Micro Food 
Processing Enterprises Scheme (PMFME), loans have been disbursed to only 252 micro 
food processing enterprises.  The Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry may 
take up the matter with concerned stakeholders  for timely disbursal of loans to the 
remaining micro food processing enterprises. 
 
 (Para 4.3.3) 
 The Committee notes the efforts taken by the Minist ry for the development of cold 
chain infrastructure. It feels that there is a scope for progress in the export and promotion 
of agricultural produce in different markets with the help of efficient cold chain storage 
and distribution facilities. The Committ ee further observes that two approved projects 
under Integrated Cold Chain and Value Addition Infrastructure Scheme of Pradhan 
Mantri Kisan SAMPADA Yojana (PMKSY) in the State of Nagaland are still under 
implementation as on 31 st January, 2023. The Committ ee therefore recommends that 
Ministry may coordinate with the concerned stakeholders  to take necessary measures 
towards operationalization of these projects at the earliest. The Committee further 
recommends that the Ministry of DoNER may take up the matter  with the Ministry of 
Food Processing Industries (MoFPI) for building more cold chain storage facilities with an 
efficient transport infrastructure support system which may boost the supply of products 
of agriculture and allied sectors into other markets. 
 (Para 4.3.4) 
Tourism  
 The Committee takes note of the Ministry of Tourism's efforts to promote tourism 
in the North East Region to make the region a preferred tourist destination. The 
Committee believes that there has been a post -COVID tourism boom aroun d the world. 
This can be best utilized by promoting tourism in NER. Every State in the North East has 
its own language, food, and cultural practices, which are beautifully represented through 
annual festivals such as the Hornbill Festival of Nagaland, the Sangai Festival of Manipur, 
the Behdienkhlam Festival of Meghalaya, and so on. Efforts may be made to make the 
journey and experience of tourists more comfortable and pleasurable so that more people 
want to visit these festivals and other attractions in th e North Eastern States. This implies 
that a seamless transportation infrastructure for tourists is required. There is also a need 
to develop a structure that allows tourists to experience this rich culture while also 

52 
 
preserving the autonomy of these tribal  areas. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry of DoNER, in collaboration with the Ministry of Tourism, focus on developing a 
mechanism to foster healthy and holistic growth in the tourism sector, thereby boosting the 
NER economy. The Committee would a lso like to be apprised about the details of 80 
infrastructure projects worth ₹ 2598.15 crores relating to water supply, power and 
connectivity which may support the tourism sector in NER. 
 (Para 4.4.2) 
 
TRANSPORT AND CONNECTIVITY 
Roadways 
The Committee believes that completing road projects on time is critical to the 
economic development of NER. The Committee takes note of various road projects carried 
out in NER under various schemes. The Committee notes with satisfaction that all the 12 
road projects sanctioned under North Eastern States Road Inves tment Programme 
(NESRIP) have been completed. The Committee notes that physical progress on many road 
projects (>₹ 300 crores) expected to be completed between 2023 and 2024 is slow. Similarly, 
the Committee also notes that, few projects under the Schemes of NEC are yet to be 
completed. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry, in collaboration with 
the NEC and MoRTH, make efforts to identify and resolve bottlenecks that are delaying 
projects so that the benefits intended for the North East can be extended as soon as 
possible. 
 
 (Para 4.5.4) 
Railways 
The Committee takes note of the progress made towards completing various railway 
projects in the NER. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of DONER in 
coordination with the M/o Railways ensure that all ongoing projects are completed within 
the time frame specified to provide NER residents with railway c onnectivity. The 
Committee would also like to know the status of the currently sanctioned project to connect 
all State capitals in the North Eastern Region, as well as the status of all other projects 
undertaken by the Northeast Frontier Railway (NFR).  
 (Para 4.6.5) 
 The Committee also notes that the delay in completing the Agartala -Akhaura rail 
link project is due to issues with the contractual agency in Bangladesh and that the Indian 
side will be completed by June 2023. The Committee recommends that all efforts be made 
to complete the Indian side work by the projected date. Furthermore, the Committee 
recommends that the matter may be taken up with the Ministry of External Affairs for 
further discussion at a higher level, so that project work gets underway  on the Bangladesh 
side. 
 (Para 4.6.6) 
Waterways 

53 
 
The Committee notes the work carried out by the Ministry for the development of 
National Waterways in NER. It may be stated that North Eastern region has a large 
potential for regional connection through wat erways and this may be optimally reaped by 
the Ministry of DoNER and the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways. 
 (Para 4.7.2) 
Civil Aviation  
The Committee notes the efforts of the Ministry of DoNER and the Ministry of Civil 
Aviation in constructing an d operationalizing a number of new airports in NER. North 
Eastern Region connectivity is a critical attribute for the region's overall development. The 
Committee also suggests that a similar impetus may be given and efforts made to 
operationalize the remai ning airports. This will help to promote tourism and last -mile 
connectivity in NER. The Committee would like to be updated on the status of the UDAN 
scheme's implementation in NER, as well as the frequency of flight operations and aircraft 
types used at these newly identified/operational airports. 
 (Para 4.8.6) 
Kaladan Multi Modal Transit Transport (KMMTT) 
 
The Committee appreciates the efforts made towards the completion of the 
waterways component of the Kaladan Multi Modal Transit Transport (KMMTT), a 
strategic connectivity project to connect the eastern ports of India with Myanmar, and all 
the works that have been done for the operationalization of the port. The Committee notes 
and hopes that since a new Project Executing Agency has been appointed for exe cution of 
the road component of KMMTT, similar commitment may be shown to realise the 
completion of road component of the project in a time bound manner.   
 
 (Para 4.9.2)

Report 
 
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the 
Ministry of Home Affairs on the recommendations contained in the Two Hundred Thirty 
Seventh Report of the Committee on Police - Training, Modernisation and Reforms. The Two 
Hundred Thirty Seventh Report was presented to the Rajya Sabha /laid on the Table of Lok 
Sabha, on 10th February, 2022. 
 
2. Action Taken Notes as received from the Ministry of Home Affairs in respect of the 
recommendations contained in the Two Hundred Thirty Seventh Report have been 
categorized as follows: 
 
Chapter I: The recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the 
Government: Para Nos. 1.4.8, 2.2.19, 2.7.4, 2.7.6, 2.11.3, 3.12.4, 3.17.4, 3.27.3, 4.3.3, 
4.4.4, 4.5.5, 4.10.7, 4.16.4 (of Two Hundred Thirty Seventh Report) 
Total recommendations- 13 Accepted. 
The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry has accepted 13 of its 
recommendations as mentioned in Chapter-I of the Report. 
 
Chapter II: The recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire 
to pursue in view of the Government’s replies: Para Nos. 2.2.15, 2.2.16, 2.2.17, 2.2.18, 
2.5.2, 2.6.4, 2.6.5, 2.7.5, 2.8.3, 2.8.4, 2.9.6, 2.9.7, 2.10.4, 2.10.5, 2.12.2, 2.13.3, 2.13.4, 
2.14.10, 2.14.12, 3.15.2, 3.15.3, 3.16.8, 3.17.3, 3.19.6, 3.19.7, 3.20.3, 3.20.4, 3.21.12, 
3.21.13, 3.25.2, 3.26.4, 4.6.12, 4.8.4, 4.9.5, 4.12.5, 4.13.9, 4.16.5,4.17.7, 4.18.2 (ibid) 
Total recommendations – 39 Not to be pursued further. 
 
The Committee is convinced with the explanations furnished by the Ministry in 
respect of 39 recommendations and, therefore, does not want to pursue the recommendations 
further. 
 
Chapter III: The recommendations/observations in respect of which the Committee is 
not satisfied with the replies of the Ministry: Para Nos. 2.2.20, 3.21.9, 3.21.10, 3.21.11, 
3.24.8, 3.27.4, 4.7.8, 4.17.8 (ibid) 
Total recommendations – 8 Not convincing replies. 
 
The Committee expresses its concern over the non-implementation of 8 of its 
recommendations contained in Chapter III and desires that the Ministry should take further 
necessary action and furnish convincing replies in respect of those recommendations within a 
time frame of three months after the presentation of the Report.  
 
Chapter IV: The recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the 
Government have not been received: Para Nos. 1.4.4, 2.3.6, 2.4.2, 2.9.8, 3.16.7, 3.17.5, 
3.18.5, 3.22.5, 3.22.6,  3.23.5, 3.24.7, 4.4.5, 4.6.9, 4.6.10,  4.6.11, 4.9.4, 4.11.5, 4.13.8, (ibid) 
Total Recommendations –18 To be pursued further. 
 
In respect of the 18 recommendations placed in Chapter IV, the Committee feels that 
the Ministry has either furnished interim replies or couched its response in vague terms. The 
Committee desires that the Ministry furnish pointed and detailed Action Taken Notes in 
respect of the recommendations categorized in Chapter IV as per the intention and spirit of 
the recommendations of the Committee within three months. 
 
 As per the categorisation indicated above, the para-wise details of the ATNs are being 
discussed in the succeeding Chapters. 
 
 

 
2 
 
CHAPTER- I 
 
Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government 
 
1.1 Ranking of Police Stations 
Recommendation/Observation  
1.1.1 The Committee appreciates the initiative of ranking of police stations in the country. 
The Committee believes that the annual ranking of police stations work as a constant guide 
for improvements. It also provides a picture of the state of physical infrastructure, resources 
and deficiencies at the level of police stations. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the MHA may incentivize the best police stations in terms of funds and resources. It will 
recognize their hard work and create an environment of healthy competition among all police 
stations in the country.  
(Para 1.4.8 of 237th  Report) 
 
Action Taken

2.1.12  Action Taken Report from Sardar Vallabh Bhai Patel National Police Academy 
(SVPNPA), Hyderabad:- 
 
a.   Training Needs Analysis: 
The Academy has been revising the training content and methodology periodically 
keeping in view of the changing field requirements. As part of this exercise, the Academy 
conducted a comprehensive Training Needs Analysis (TNA) in the year 2020 with the 
objective to understand the gap in domain knowledge, skills and attitudes imparted during 
training to the IPS recruits at the Academy vis-à-vis the requirements in the field. 
 

 
13 
 
In this massive exercise, the Academy collected about 12000 responses from eight 
states (Assam, Delhi, Gujarat, Kerala, Odisha, Punjab, Rajasthan, and Telangana) by using 
customized questionnaires, not only from uniformed officers and personnel of all ranks 
(approx. 700 from each state), but also from the allied departments and citizens across the 
cross-section of society (about 400 from each state), from the IPS officers of previous ten 
batches (61-70 RR batch) and the trainer SPs/SSPs of IPS Probationers of the last five 
batches (66-70 RR batch). All these have been analyzed to identify the gaps in basic training. 
In addition, the responses of the National Security Advisor, Union Home Secretary, Senior 
Security Advisor, Director Intelligence Bureau, Director CBI, Secretary R&AW, Director 
General BPR&D, DGs of CAPFs (CRPF, BSF, CISF, NSG) and DGs of various state police 
formations (Assam, Chhattisgarh, Haryana, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Odisha, Punjab and 
Telangana) were also incorporated. 
 
Committees consisting of senior police officers and academicians were constituted on 
Indoor training, Outdoor training and Teaching methodologies for discussing the insights 
obtained from the Training Need Analysis to identify actionable points and suggest changes 
to be brought about in the Basic Course training. Subsequently, presentations were made 
before the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA). MHA has permitted the Academy to implement 
the findings of the TNA exercise for the Basic Course training of 73 RR Batch (2020 batch of 
IPS). 
 
b. Academy’s supervision during the District Practical Training: 
A system of appointing a faculty member as counselor to each of the IPS probationers 
is in place at the Academy. The faculty counselor will be in touch with the IPS Probationer 
during the phase 1 training at the National Police Academy, District Practical Training 
(DPT) at the corresponding cadre state of the probationer and during the phase training at 
the National Police Academy. 
 
Further, it is to submit that, the faculty coordinators remain in close contact with the 
probationer throughout his/her training and also remain in touch with both the probationer 
and Training SP through video conferencing. As suggested by the Parliamentary committee 
counselors have been visiting the probationers in the field and also getting feedback so as to 
improve training. 
 
c. Mentor scheme:    In addition to the above the National Police Academy started the Mentor 
system from 2020 onwards. 
 
All the states have appointed mentors to guide the officer trainees during the period of 
their District Practical Training and beyond. 
 
The idea behind the mentorship is that in the initial phases of getting used to the life 
of a police officer, the officer trainees face a lot of professional & personal dilemmas which 
need to be addressed for imparting the right values & attitudes for a career of integrity, 
professionalism and contribution to the society. 
 
Every state would have some officers, who have proven themselves in the field and 
are known for their professionalism and integrity. If some of these officers, in the rank of SP/ 
SSP / DIG, are appointed as the mentors exclusively (apart from trainer SPs) for the officer 
trainees, then grooming them during the DPT, and even thereafter, would progress in the 
right direction and these Mentors might be able to shape them in their own mould. This 
scheme has been operationalised from 73 RR. 
 
 

 
14 
 
d.  Ethical Dilemmas: 
The Academy follows a sandwich model of training where in phase 1 training for 46 
weeks is imparted at the Academy, followed by 29 weeks of district practical training at the 
respective cadre state. After the district practical training, the trainee will report back to the 
Academy for 12 week phase 2 training. Phase 2 training is the final part of the basic course 
training. In the phase 2 training, there is a special module conducted on clearing the ethical 
dilemmas faced by the IPS Probationers during the field training. All aspects including 
integrity, honesty, rule of law, compassion, welfare etc. are discussed in this module. 
 
Further recommendation  
2.1.13 The Committee notes the reply.

2.6 Training to deal with Cyber Crime 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.6.1 The Committee expresses its concern on the increasing rate of cyber crimes in the 
country. As per the NCRB data, cyber crime cases have increased from 27248 in 2018 to 
50035 in 2020. The Committee observes that these crimes are mainly related to financial 
transactions. The criminals not only target the innocent and vulnerable, especially elderly 
people, and dupe them of their savings but also well-known persons and celebrities. The 
Committee is of the view that specialized training is required to deal with the increasing 
cyber crimes in the country. The Committee recommends that the SVPNPA, NEPA should 
coordinate with State training academies to train police personnel with requisite knowledge 
of cyber laws, cyber crime investigation, digital forensics and upgrade them from time to 
time on new technological tools to deal with cyber crimes. The training academies may be 
advised to recruit cyber experts as trainers on cyber technologies. 
(Para 2.9.6  ibid) 
Action Taken 
Action Taken Report from SVPNPA :- 
 
2.6.2 SVP National Police Academy is the premier police training academy in the country 
mandated to train IPS officers for their basic course and mid-career/senior courses. 
2.6.3 SVP National Police Academy, with a vision for tackling growing cyber-crime, set up 
National Digital Crime Resource and Training Centre (NDCRTC) in the year 2015 under its 
IT wing.  The initial technical support and guidance were provided by CDAC (Hyderabad).  
The centre aims for Capacity building of Law Enforcement Agencies in Cyber Crime 
Investigation.  This Centre is mandated to train officers from State Police, CPOs and other 
LEAs of the Central Government, Digital Forensic Experts of CFSL and State FSL, Judges 
and Prosecutors.  The main objective of this Centre is to train all stakeholders in the field of 
Cyber Crime Investigation and in creating a pool of Master Trainers in this field in all wings 
of the Criminal Justice System across the Country in association with different agencies of 
State as well as Central Government working in this field. 
2.6.4 NDCRTC in the past 6 years of its existence has conducted more than 200 training 
courses for police officers, judicial officers, prosecutors and officers from other services like 
revenue, forest and customs.  It also trained foreign police officers from friendly nations like 
Bhutan, Maldives, Mauritius, Nepal, Sierra Leone and other BIMSTEC countries.  NDCRTC 
conducts training not only at the Academy campus in Hyderabad, but also travels across the 
country to various States to train officers of State/Central/International Law enforcement 
agencies.  During such courses, the NDCRTC team interacts with the participants and 

 
19 
 
identifies the key problems fact by the investigating officers in the field while handling 
various cases related to the field of Cybercrime investigation. 
2.6.5 All these problems are adequately incorporated and the training modules are 
designed in such a manner as to cover and address these practical issues found on the 
ground.  The courses are always kept dynamic and relevant to every changing field level 
challenges.   NDCRTS also helps investigation officers in solving crimes by providing 
guidance and suggestions on technical aspects during the investigation. 
2.6.6 This experience gained by the NDCRTC team aids in improving the course content 
thus making it more appropriate to cutting-edge police officers. 
2.6.7 NDCRTC has organized various courses related to Cyber Crime Investigation, Cyber 
Forensics, Cyber Security to the benefit of various law enforcement agencies both at the 
National Police Academy and in other State/Central Police Academies.  The centre offers 
both physical and online courses for the benefit of the participants. 
2.6.8 The experts of NDCRTC have travelled across the length and breadth of the country 
and organized these courses at the doorstep of state police establishments and central 
organization.  NDCRTC successfully trained the trainers and the personnel at all ranks in 
these agencies, thereby contributing greatly to the capacity building of these units in tackling 
Cybercrimes.

i. Cyber Crime and Cyber Law for Judicial Officers and Prosecutors in years 2021 and 
2022 in which a total of 86 officers participated. 
ii.  Dark Web and Crypto Currency Investigation in which 45 officers attended.

2.6.14 “Police” and “Public Order” are State subjects, as per the Seventh Schedule of the

2.6.15 The MHA has rolled out ‘Cyber Crime Volunteer Framework’ as a part of cyber

siphoned off by fraudsters. A Toll-free Helpline Number ‘1930’ has been operationalized to

relieving officials from active duty for training purposes. This will ensure that the officials

3.2 Investigation of Cyber Crimes 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.2.1  The Committee expresses its deep concerns over the rising rate of cyber crimes in the 
country. As per the information provided to the Committee, it is seen that some of the States 
like Punjab, Rajasthan, Goa, Assam do not have a single cyber crime cell, while in Andhra 
Pradesh, Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh, only one/two cyber crime cells have been set up. It 
observes that each day, cyber-criminals are using newer methods and new modus-operandi to 
commit cyber crimes. Therefore, it is important for the police to stay updated on new modus-
operandi and technology trends adopted by criminals. 
(Para 3.21.9  ibid) 
 
3.2.2  The Committee recommends that MHA may advise States to set up cyber cells in all 
the districts. The States should map the cyber crime hotspots which will help in quick 
detection of crimes and taking proactive measures to prevent cyber crimes. 
(Para 3.21.10 ibid) 
 
3.2.3 The Committee also recommends to upgrade the existing cyber cells by setting up dark 
web monitoring cells and social media monitoring cells to tackle different types of cyber 
crimes. 
(Para 3.21.11 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
3.2.4 Cyber space is a borderless, complex and dynamic environment. The complexity of 
digitalization allows criminals to take advantage in committing cyber crimes like financial 
fraud, ransomware, malware attacks, identity theft, data theft, privacy breach, etc. The 
increase in the number of internet users, clubbed with rapid digital service adoption and low 
cyber literacy has led to an increase in cyber crimes incidents across the country.   Evolving 
technology like, the Internet of Things (IoT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), Drones, etc., may 
bring new challenges to cyber space. 
 
3.2.5 “Police” and “Public Order” are State subjects, as per the Seventh Schedule of the 
Constitution of India. States/UTs are primarily responsible for the prevention, detection, 
investigation, prosecution of crimes and capacity building of their Local enforcement 
Agencies (LEAs) including, setting up of district cyber cell, dark web monitoring cell, social 
media monitoring cell, training of LEA personnel etc., to deal with cyber crime. The Central 
Government supplements the initiatives of the State/UT Governments through advisories and 
financial assistance under various schemes for their capacity building. The MHA has issued 
an advisory to all the State/UT Governments for setting up State and District Cyber Crime 
Cells, in each State/UT for the handling of all types of cyber crimes. Accordingly, all 

 
37 
 
States/UTs, including Punjab, Rajasthan, Goa & Assam, have also set up a dedicated Cyber 
Crime Cell as Nodal Point to handle cyber crimes. 
3.2.6 The MHA has established ‘Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C)’ to 
provide a framework and eco-system for the LEAs to deal with cyber crimes in a 
comprehensive and coordinated manner. 
 
Further recommendation  
3.2.7 The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry that dedicated Cyber Cells have 
been set up in all the State/UT Governments including Punjab, Rajasthan, Goa and 
Assam which did not have a single cyber crime cell earlier.  The Committee further 
notes that the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) has been set up by the 
Ministry to deal with cyber crimes in a comprehensive and coordinated manner.   
  
3.2.8 The Committee recommends that the Ministry may encourage State 
Governments to identify cyber hotspots in their State and maintain data profile on the 
cyber crimes being committed in those hotspot and the measures taken to contain those 
crimes. This data in this regard may be collected by the ‘Indian Cyber Crime 
Coordination Centre (I4C)’ and shared with other States for framing of policies by 
them to tackle such types of cyber crimes.

Recommendation/Observation 
4.2.1 From the information provided by the States, the Committee understands that the 
States have their own training institutes that are imparting training to the State police 
personnel. The Committee also notes that as on 1st January, 2020, there are 203 police 
training institutes in the country. The Committee recommends that the MHA may take up 
with States/UTs to scale up the training capacity of all training institutions in the country to 
enhance their infrastructure with virtual classrooms, cyber labs and also to develop a few 
training centres as 'Centre of Excellence' for certain specific subjects relating to the police 
system. This will also facilitate training opportunities to the maximum number of police 
personnel in the States. The MHA may also allocate adequate funds and resources for the

4.4 Training to deal with Cyber Crime 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.4.1 The Committee, hence, recommends that the MHA may allocate adequate funds and 
extend necessary resources for the establishment of cyber training labs and 
strengthening/upgrading of existing cyber training infrastructure in all the States/UTs. 
(Para 2.9.8 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
4.4.2 Though “Police” and “Public Order” are State subjects, MHA has taken several 
steps to enhance the capacity building of the States/UTs LEAs to handle the cyber crime 
cases, which inter-alia, include the following:- 
 Financial assistance provided under the ‘Cyber Crime Prevention against Women and 
Children (CCPWC)’ Scheme to the States/UTs for setting up of cyber forensic-cum-
training laboratories, hiring of junior consultants and training of law enforcement 
agencies personnel, public prosecutors and judicial officers. So far, 28 States/UTs have 
operationalized the Cyber Forensic-cum-Training Laboratories. 
 The MHA has prepared 3/5/10 days training programs for law enforcement agencies, 
Public Prosecutors and Judicial Officers for improving cyber crime awareness, in 
consultation with the stakeholders and States/UTs are mandated to organize training 
programs. So far, more than 19900 Officials, which include 17345 Police personnel, 
1054 Judicial Officers and 1532 Public Prosecutors have been trained. 
 The National Cyber Forensic Laboratory (NCFL), a ‘State of the Art’ facility has been 
set up to train & assist the State/UT Investigation Officers. The NCFL has been made 
functional and its facilities are being extended to the States/UTs. Services in more than 
4,600 cases have been provided to the State LEAs in cyber forensics investigations of 
cases. 
 The Massive Open Online Courses (MOOC) platform under the 14C called ‘CyTrain’ 
portal has been developed. CyTrain portal helps in the capacity building of Police 
Officers/Judicial Officers through online courses on critical aspects of cyber crime 
investigation, forensics, prosecution etc. along with certification. More than 12,200 
Police Officers from States/UTs are registered and more than 300 Certificates issued 
through the portal. 
 State of the art “e-Cyber Lab” has been established with more than 25 latest Digital 
Forensics tools from the industry and more than 50 open-source cyber crime detection 
and forensics tools and integrated with the CyTrain portal for providing virtual 
experience on experimenting with the latest modus operandi on cyber crime. 
 Workshops for Law Enforcement Authorities on the functioning of the National Cyber 
Crime Reporting Portal (www.cybercime.gov.in) are organized by the NCRB to provide 
hands-on training to the participants for taking appropriate action on complaints 
reported through the Portal. 
 More than 2000 police Officials working in cyber cells across the country have been 
trained on Crypto currency, forensics, investigation etc. 
4.4.3 The Directorate of Forensic Science Services (DFSS) has been assigned to set up 
NCFL at Hyderabad for evidentiary purpose. Establishment of this laboratory will provide 
the necessary forensic support to the LEAs in preserving the evidence and its analysis in line

4.5 Standardization of Equipments, Weaponry, Vehicles, etc. 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.5.1 The Committee is of the view that modern policing requires strong communication 
support, state-of-the-art  modern weapons, and a high degree of mobility for quick 
response.The Committee notes with anguish that 257 police stations do not have vehicles, 
638 police stations do not have telephones and 143 police stations are not having 
wireless/mobiles in the country. In the 21st century India, there are police stations without 
telephones or proper wireless connectivity especially in many sensitive states like Arunachal 
Pradesh, Odisha and Punjab, particularly in view of the fact that some of these States had 
been rewarded with better performance incentives in the year 2018-19. Further, a very 
sensitive border Union Territory like Jammu & Kashmir also has a sizeable number of police 
stations which does not have telephones and wireless sets. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the MHA may advise such States to immediately equip their police stations 
with adequate vehicles and communication devices else it may lead to disincentivization of 
modernisation grants from the Centre. For the UTs, MHA may ensure that the needful is done 
at the earliest. 
(Para 3.16.7 ibid) 
Action Taken

Governments, with the request to take appropriate action to immediately equip their police 
stations with adequate vehicles and communication devices. 
Further recommendation  
4.5.3 The Committee notes the reply that States/UT Governments have been advised 
to take appropriate action on the recommendation of the Committee to equip the police 
stations with adequate infrastructure immediately.  The Committee would like to be

4.7 Installation of CCTV Cameras in Police Stations 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.7.1 The Committee notes that some of the States/UTs have started installing  CCTV 
cameras in police stations to comply with the directions of the Hon'ble Supreme Court. It 
appreciates that Tamil Nadu Police has installed IP CCTV cameras which enables a senior 
police official to keep an eye on the activities inside the police station. It observes that such a 
measure is a good step towards protecting the rights and legal remedies of the citizens while 
they are in the police station to file their complaints, FIRs, etc., and ensuring that there is no 
harassment on the part of police staff. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may 
take up with the States/UTs for installing at least one or two IP cameras at a strategic location 
in all police stations. The Committee also recommends that States/UTs may conduct a 
periodic audit of all the CCTVs installed in police stations and replace/upgrade them, 
wherever required.  The Committee further recommends that the MHA take up with the 
Ministry of Law & Justice to advise States/UTs to initiate talks with their respective courts 
for installation of CCTVs at court premises, for round-the-clock monitoring of court 
buildings.  
(Para 3.18.5 ibid)

4.8 Efforts to Tackle Drone Attacks 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.8.1 The Committee expresses its grave concern on the use of different types of drones for 
committing crimes, transporting drugs, arms and ammunition, etc., which is a threat to the 
internal security of the country. The Committee notes that the MHA has issued guidelines for 
flying permission in red, green and yellow zones. The Committee recommends that the MHA 
along with the Ministry of Civil Aviation may advise States to sensitize ground-level police 
personnel on the drone regulations. This may include the civilian use of drones which will 
help in detecting rogue drones. 
(Para 3.22.5 ibid) 
4.8.2 The Committee also recommends that the MHA may take up with concerned 
Ministries/ Agencies to create a central pool of anti-drone technology at the earliest and give 
its access to all States/UTs to deal with the menace of illicit use of drones. For this purpose, 
the participation of the private sector may be explored. The MHA may coordinate with 
concerned Ministries/Agencies and States/UTs to create an SOP for the steps to be taken by 
the State police in case of a drone attack. 
(Para 3.22.6 ibid) 
Action Taken 
4.8.3 Ministry of Home Affairs has already issued an SOP to all the States/UTs vide O.M. 
dated 10.05.2019. National Counter Rogue Drone Policy and Guidelines (NCRDPG) are 
being finalized. 
 
4.8.4 The draft National Counter Rogue Drone Policy and Guidelines (NCRDPG) are 
being finalized which visualizes the threat concerns mentioned in this para and suitable 
provisions are proposed in respect of these issues. 
 
 
Further recommendation  
  
4.8.5 The Committee notes that the Government is in the process of finalizing the 
National Counter Rogue Drone Policy and Guidelines (NCRDPG).  The Committee 
believes that adequate provisions will be integrated into these guidelines to counter the 
challenges to internal security due to use of drones to carry out illicit activities, such as 
smuggling of drugs, guns, ammunition, etc. The Committee may be informed about 
these guidelines after finalization. 
 
4.9 Vacancies in the State Police Forces 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.9.1  The Committee notes the vacancy of 5,31,737 as against the sanctioned strength of 
26,23,225 in State police forces, is almost  21 % shortfall. It is not a desirable figure given the 
crime and security scenario in the country. The Committee is of the considered view that 
shortage of staff has a direct bearing on the efficiency of the police. The workload of the 
existing staff increases forcing them to do work overtime, most of the time in stressful and 
trying circumstances. This not only leads to the increased stress level of police venting out at 
times on common people but also compromises the overall performance of police in the 
discharge of their duties. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the MHA may advise 
States/UTs to conduct Police recruitment drives in a mission mode and remove the

administrative bottlenecks for the recruitment of police personnel at different ranks in a time-
bound manner.  
(Para 3.23.5 ibid) 
Action Taken

Constitution of India. It is primarily the responsibility of the State Governments/Union 
Territories (UTs) to fill up the vacant posts in their respective police force. This Ministry had 
been issuing advisories to the States/UTs from time to time in this regard. An advisory in this 
regard has been issued to all the States/UTs relating to filling up vacancies in the police

4.10 Women Representation on Police 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.10.1 The Committee is anguished to note that women are abysmally under-represented in 
the police force as they constitute only 10.30% of the police force. The Committee 
recommends that the MHA may advise States/UTs to create a roadmap for making the 
representation of women police to 33% of the total strength a reality. Further, the 
appointment of women in police may be done by creating additional posts rather than 
converting the vacant posts of male constables. It will also help in improving the police-
population ratio in the country. Besides increasing the percentage of women in police,  taking 
a cue from the defense forces where women are being assigned combative roles, the MHA 
may also advise the States/UTs to give them important challenging duties central to the 
police, and not just duties of inconsequence.  
(Para 3.24.7 ibid) 
Action Taken 
4.10.2 “Police” is a State subject falling in List-II (State List) of the Seventh Schedule of the 
Constitution of India. It is primarily the responsibility of the State Governments/Union 
Territories (UTs) to make efforts to increase women’s representation in the police force.  
This Ministry had been issuing advisories to the States/UTs from time to time in this regard.

4.12 Separation of Investigation from law and order  
Recommendation/Observation 
4.12.1 The Committee notes that only a few States have separated the investigation from the 
law and order duties of their police. The Committee is of the view that separation of 
investigation from law and order is important to maintain the accountability of the police and 
increase their autonomy in investigating crimes. Therefore, the Committee recommends that 
the MHA may advise the remaining States to create separate investigations and law and order 
wings in the police. It will lead to specialization and professionalism in the police 
department, speed up the investigation and secure the conviction of offenders. 
(Para 4.6.9 ibid) 
4.12.2   To address the shortage of staff in creating separate wings for investigation and law 
& order, the Committee recommends that the personnel of the rank of ASIs & head 
constables can be utilized for investigation of minor offences of simple nature after adequate 
training. 
(Para 4.6.10 ibid) 
 
4.12.3   The Committee notes that one of the reasons of low conviction rate is the lapses in 
the investigation. Therefore, it is important that regular monitoring and supervision of the 
investigation of cases should be done by senior officers. The Committee recommends that the 
MHA may advise States for the field visit of the senior police officers of the rank of 
SP/IG/DIG for on-the-spot assessment of investigation of cases. The SP/DSP should submit 
monthly PRs (Progress Reports) on important cases and the performance of I/Os. 
Accordingly, suitable rewards/punishment should also be given to I/Os. The Committee also 
recommends to upgrade the skills of the I/Os through periodic training and engaging experts 
as and when necessary. 
(Para 4.6.11 ibid) 
 
 

 
48 
 
Action Taken 
4.12.4 “Police” is a State subject falling in List-II (State List) of the Seventh Schedule of the 
Constitution of India. It is primarily the responsibility of the State Governments/Union 
Territories (UTs) to take necessary action regarding the separation of investigation from law 
and order. The advisory in this regard has been issued to all the States/UTs vide letter dated 
27.04.2022. 
Further Recommendation  
4.12.5 The Committee notes the reply and recommends that the Ministry should follow 
up with the State Governments/UTs on the action taken in response to the advisory 
issued by it.

Recommendation/Observation 
4.14.1 The Committee notes that according to MHA, the State Governments are responsible 
to ensure the career progression of their police personnel. However, the promotional aspect is 
a very important aspect of police reform on which the Union Government is in contact with 
the State Government. The Committee further notes that the system of promotion of 
constables is different in the States and observes that most of the States do not follow 
incentive linked promotion schemes or any kind of extraordinary performance-linked 
promotion schemes. The Committee recommends that MHA may encourage States to

incentive-linked promotion schemes to keep them motivated.

4.15 Independent Police Complaint Authority 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.15.1  The Committee notes that 31 States/UTs have constituted Police Complaints 
Authorities at the State and District levels for looking into complaints against police officers. 
The Committee is of the view that the Police Complaint Authority should be established 
outside the police force. Therefore, The Committee recommends that the MHA along with 
the Ministry of Law & Justice may take up with States to ensure that the Police Complaint 
Authority should comprise of retired High Court Judges, retired senior civil servant/ police 
officers, eminent jurists along with the representation of women. The Committee also 
recommends that BPR&D may conduct a study to assess the effectiveness of the Independent 
Police Complaint Authority in States to check whether the complaints against police 
personnel have gone up or reduced. The study may also include the types of complaints 
against police personnel and action taken thereon.  
(Para 4.13.8 ibid)
